summary: The "which weights get how many bits" problem is well-studied offline (HAWQ lineage → Hessian/Fisher sensitivity → ILP/knapsack under a size budget), and as of late 2025/2026 the *online, serving-time* version of the idea has been published at least twice — DynaExq (arXiv:2511.15015) is almost exactly the proposed "fungible quant" for MoE (EMA expert-hotness from live router traces → budget-constrained top-N precision set → async promote/demote via pointer-indirection "stable expert handles" over fixed-block memory pools), and MorphServe (arXiv:2506.02006) demonstrates ~6 ms hot-swap of quantized layers inside a live serving engine by pre-staging variants in pinned CPU memory and writing into pre-reserved fixed-size GPU slots. Both solve the exact objections raised (atomic swap memory, fragmentation, "vLLM loads weights once") with mechanisms that transfer directly. The single most consequential finding for this specific stack is negative: the "one artifact, many bit-widths" nesting literature (Any-Precision LLM, MatQuant, AnyBCQ, RRQ, Drop-by-Drop) all relies on integer MSB-slicing, bit-planes, or additive residual codebooks — and QTIP/EXL3 trellis codes are explicitly **not** successively refinable, because each weight group decodes from a sliding L-bit window of the bitstream and truncating the rate destroys Viterbi optimality. So K4→K3 in EXL3 requires a real re-encode or a second stored copy; the free-truncation shortcut does not exist for Trellis without changing the codec. Two further findings should reshape the allocation policy: EvoPress (arXiv:2410.14649, ICML 2025) shows empirically that per-layer error is **not** monotone/additive, which invalidates naive greedy-knapsack allocation; and TASA (arXiv:2607.00908) shows perplexity-based layer sensitivity has Kendall τ ≈ 0 with reasoning-task sensitivity, and that calibrating on *pure* in-domain data actively degrades quality (degenerate Hessian eigenspectrum) — a direct warning against a quant that over-specializes to one user's traffic. Finally, the assumption that allocation requires BF16 activation measurement on rented B300s is contradicted by three calibration-free/cheap metrics: HT-SR spectral alpha (AlphaQ), router L2-norm (arXiv:2604.06515, "no GPU and negligible computation"), and forward-only KL sensitivity (arXiv:2604.13440, no backprop, no Hessian).

findings.title: DynaExq — the proposed idea, already published, for MoE expert precision (closest prior art by far)
findings.detail: "Dynamic Expert Quantization for Scalable Mixture-of-Experts Inference", Kexin Chu, Dawei Xiang, Zixu Shen, Yiwei Yang, Zecheng Lin, Wei Zhang (UConn / UCSC), arXiv:2511.15015 (v3). Frames single-GPU MoE inference under a hard HBM envelope as an *online, budget-constrained precision allocation problem*. Mechanism: (1) per-expert selection counters from live router traces, smoothed by EMA over fixed time windows, S[l,e] ← α·S[l,e] + (1−α)·c[l,e]; (2) per-layer budget-feasible top-N rule H[l] ← TopN({S[l,e]}, n_hi,l) after reserving fixed memory for non-expert weights; (3) **"stable expert handles"** — an immutable handle identity holding a pointer to the currently-active GPU version, so promotion/demotion swaps the pointer after the copy completes, never mid-forward; (4) migration runs on a dedicated CUDA stream (stream_mig) with CUDA-event publication, so "the forward pass does not wait for this transfer... it continues to use the current active version via the stable handle"; (5) fragmentation handled by *partitioned fixed-granularity pools* (pool_hi, pool_lo) with constant-time freelists, blocks aligned to expert-size granularity; (6) hysteresis — an expert must enter a slightly wider candidate set before becoming eligible — to stop thrashing. Precisions: FP16 hot / INT4 or INT2 cold, using existing PTQ (no new quantizer). ~3K lines of Python on HuggingFace Transformers + PyTorch, RTX A6000 48GB, Qwen3-30B/80B and Phi-3.5-MoE. Results: Qwen3-80B accuracy 73.09% (static INT2) → 77.57% at the same memory budget; up to 2.73× throughput vs offloading/prefetch baselines at batch 32; TTFT/TPOT near static quantization.
findings.relevance: This is the fungible-quant idea, minus the re-encode step. It answers every objection raised: the atomic-swap memory problem is solved by pointer indirection behind a stable handle (no pre-reserved double buffer per tensor, just two pools); fragmentation is solved by fixed-block partitioned pools rather than the caching allocator; slow reaction is handled by EMA + hysteresis on a background stream. Crucially it *sidesteps the size-change problem entirely* by keeping two pre-quantized versions per expert in separate size-homogeneous pools rather than re-encoding — which is the design most likely to work for EXL3 given trellis codes cannot be truncated. Weaknesses to exploit: it is single-GPU, built on HF Transformers not vLLM, uses FP16/INT4/INT2 not sub-4-bit trellis, and never re-encodes, so its "budget" is coarse (an expert is either hot or cold). It also does not address TP/DCP sharding at all.

findings.title: MorphServe — runtime quantized-layer hot-swapping inside a live LLM serving engine, with measured swap latency
findings.detail: "MorphServe: Efficient and Workload-Aware LLM Serving via Runtime Quantized Layer Swapping and KV Cache Resizing", Zhaoyuan Su, Zeyu Zhang, Tingfeng Lan, Zirui Wang, Haiying Shen, Juncheng Yang, Yue Cheng. arXiv:2506.02006 (v1 May 2025, v2 Jan 2026). Mechanics: pre-quantized layer variants (FP16/INT8/INT4/INT3) are staged in **pinned CPU memory** before serving; the FP16 replica sits in *preallocated* GPU memory; the system tracks memory addresses of every variant so a swap is a direct memory copy. Quantized variants are copied **into identical memory addresses** so no pointer remapping is needed; the FP16 layer is simply discarded from GPU since a pinned-CPU backup exists. Swaps run on **asynchronous CUDA streams**, giving "state-preserving transitions with minimum runtime overhead." Measured on Llama-2-7B / PCIe Gen4: INT4 layer transfer ~4 ms, FP16 layer transfer ~16 ms, full swap including reconstruction **~6 ms, fully overlapped with decoding (negligible TPOT overhead)**. Layer choice uses a Layer Importance Score combining Layer Transformation Sensitivity, Layer Replacement Sensitivity and Model Degradation Sensitivity (α1=α2=0.25, β=0.5). Built on SwiftLLM (~2,200 LoC Python + 500 LoC C++/CUDA), compatible with PagedAttention/FlashAttention. Memory: FP16→INT4 saves up to 75% per layer (~0.4 GB → ~0.1 GB on Llama-2-7B); freed memory is handed to the KV cache by a "KVResizer", expanding KVC by up to 32.97% beyond the full-precision limit, cutting queueing delay up to 3.8×, reducing SLO violations 92.45% and improving P95 TTFT 2.2–3.9×.
findings.relevance: Direct rebuttal to "vLLM loads weights ONCE at startup, so runtime weight replacement needs heavy lifting" — it has been done, in a paged-attention serving engine, at ~6 ms per layer fully hidden behind decode. Two mechanisms are directly stealable: (a) **write the smaller quantized tensor into the pre-reserved larger FP16-sized slot** so the tensor's base pointer never changes — this is the cheapest possible answer to the EPLB size-asymmetry problem, at the cost of internal fragmentation equal to the size delta; (b) pinned-CPU staging of the alternate bit-width so the GPU-side critical section is a single async D2H/H2D memcpy. It also validates that freed weight memory can be recycled into KV-cache blocks, which matters a lot on 96 GB cards with no NVLink.

findings.title: BLOCKER: QTIP/EXL3 trellis codes are NOT successively refinable — a K4 code does not contain a K3 code
findings.detail: QTIP: "Quantization with Trellises and Incoherence Processing", Albert Tseng et al., arXiv:2406.11235, NeurIPS 2024. EXL3 is documented by turboderp as "a streamlined variant of QTIP" (exllamav3/doc/exl3.md). In the bitshift trellis, k is bits *per edge* and L is the state size (e.g. L=16, k=2, V=1); decoding is a sliding-window operation — "the t-th [group] only depends on bit positions {(t−1)kV+1, …, (t−1)kV+L}", i.e. each group of V weights decodes from a contiguous L-bit window of the bitstream. Fetching the paper and asking directly about embedded/successive refinability: the trellis structure does **not** support truncation to extract a k−1-bit approximation; the Viterbi search finds an optimal path through a rate-specific trellis graph, and truncating bits breaks that optimality with no guarantee of a valid coarser representation. Classical coding theory agrees that TCQ is not naturally successively refinable — embedded TCQ (E-TCQ) and "successively refinable trellis coded quantization" (US Patent 6,125,149) exist precisely because the plain construction is not refinable, and they change the code. QTIP reference numbers: Llama-2-70B WikiText2 PPL 3.78 @ 2-bit, 3.26 @ 3-bit, 3.16 @ 4-bit. Ancestry: QuIP arXiv:2307.13304 → QuIP# arXiv:2402.04396 (randomized Hadamard incoherence + E8 lattice codebooks) → QTIP (trellis, dimension >100 at linear cost).
findings.relevance: This is the finding that most changes the design. The hypothesis in the brief — "if a K4 weight can be truncated to K3 with no re-encode, the whole hot-swap problem changes character" — is FALSE for EXL3 as it stands. Every free-truncation scheme in the literature (Any-Precision LLM, MatQuant, AnyBCQ, MoBiQuant) is built on either integer MSB nesting, bit-plane decomposition, or additive residual codebooks; none is a trellis. So for GLM-5.2 + EXL3 the realistic options are: (1) store both K3 and K4 encodings (DynaExq-style two-pool residency, paying disk/host RAM not VRAM), (2) re-encode on a background stream (Viterbi + Hessian per tensor — the expensive path), or (3) change codec for the fungible tensors to something additively refinable (RRQ / Drop-by-Drop / AnyBCQ style) and accept a quality gap vs trellis at a given bpw. Worth checking directly against the exllamav3 quantizer source: the only public hook found was `bits_per_weight = shape[-1] // 16` in exllamav3/conversion/quant_config.py, and turboderp explicitly defers the format spec to the code ("A full description of the format is coming").

findings.title: Any-Precision LLM — one stored artifact served at 3..n bits with zero re-encode, via bit-plane layout (the canonical nesting result)
findings.detail: "Any-Precision LLM: Low-Cost Deployment of Multiple, Different-Sized LLMs", Yeonhong Park, Jake Hyun, SangLyul Cho, Bonggeun Sim, Jae W. Lee (SNU), arXiv:2402.10517, ICML 2024. Two parts. (a) **Incremental upscaling**: start from a seed model at the lowest precision (e.g. 3-bit) and add one bit at a time; "all parameters of the n_i-bit model are inherited to the n_{i+1}-bit model, and a single additional bit is appended to the end of each parameter." With SqueezeLLM's clustering backbone, upscaling splits each cluster into two sub-centroids via weighted k-means. (b) **Bit-plane memory layout**: weights are stored as n separate bit-vectors (bit 0 of all weights in one array, bit 1 in another, …) rather than bit-packed per weight. Consequence: "any runtime request of reduced bit-width directly translates into proportional speedup, as we can simply load the specified amount of bits" — serving at 4 bits from an 8-bit parent means fetching bitplanes 4–7 plus the 4-bit centroid table. **No re-encoding.** Lookup tables for all supported bit-widths stay resident simultaneously. Custom CUDA kernel: load bitplanes → bit-transpose (~40 bitwise ops vs 76 naive) → shift/mask to build LUT indices → shared-memory centroid fetch → MAC; plus byte-level bitplane permutation for coalescing and 3-bit adjacent-index merging into 6-bit lookups. RTX 4090 matvec: 3.99× vs FP16 cuBLAS at 3-bit, 3.03× at 4-bit, 1.56× at 8-bit. **Critical caveat:** the method requires a *non-uniform, clustering-based* backbone. Table 2 shows uniform quantizers fail catastrophically under incremental upscaling — AWQ + incremental upscaling produces INF perplexity at 4-bit.
findings.relevance: This is the existence proof that the hot-swap problem *can* be made trivial — but only if the codec is chosen for it. If the fungible tensors were re-encoded to a bit-plane non-uniform LUT format instead of trellis, then K3↔K4 becomes a change to a length field and an LUT pointer, with zero VRAM churn, zero fragmentation, zero atomicity problem, and the 'upgrade' direction costs only the extra bitplane's bandwidth. The tradeoff is quality: SqueezeLLM-style scalar LUT at 3 bpw is materially worse than EXL3/QTIP trellis at 3 bpw. That is the real design decision — trade ~a few tenths of PPL for O(1)-cost runtime bit mobility. Also note this scheme makes the *storage* cost equal to the max bit-width, so K3/K4 mixing costs K4 on disk but only the used planes in VRAM.

findings.title: MatQuant / Matryoshka Quantization — MSB-slicing an int8 model into int4/int2, but requires co-training
findings.detail: "Matryoshka Quantization", Pranav Nair, Puranjay Datta, Jeff Dean, Prateek Jain, Aditya Kusupati (Google DeepMind), arXiv:2502.06786, **ICLR 2025 Oral**. Exploits the fact that integer types are inherently nested: int4 and int2 live in the most significant bits of int8. Trains/quantizes a single model with **co-training and co-distillation regularization across bit-widths simultaneously**, so that all MSB slices are individually good. Compatible with OmniQuant and QAT as base algorithms (a MatGPTQ variant appears in follow-up work). Results: int2 models extracted by MatQuant beat standard int2 by up to 4% (OmniQuant base) and 7% (QAT base); an "effective 2.05-bit" variant using one extra bit for outliers adds another ~6%. Naive MSB slicing of an independently-quantized int8 model does *not* work well — the co-training is what makes the nested slices usable.
findings.relevance: Establishes the theoretical ceiling and the practical cost of nesting: nesting is not free, you pay for it in the quantization procedure (co-training / co-distillation), and the low-bit slices are worse than a dedicated low-bit quant unless you explicitly optimize for them. For a fungible-quant design this means the artifact must be *built* fungible from the start — you cannot retrofit fungibility onto an existing K4 EXL3 tensor. It also means the 'downgrade' path (K3←K4) is where quality is lost, and MatQuant's co-distillation is the known mitigation. Note this is offline-only: the allocation is not decided, only the *representation* is made sliceable; a serving-time policy still has to choose the slice.

findings.title: Additive/residual multi-precision codecs — RRQ, Drop-by-Drop, AnyBCQ, MoBiQuant: precision switching by adding or dropping summands
findings.detail: Four independent 2025–2026 lines that make precision switching free without integer MSB nesting. (1) **RRQ**, "Recurrent Residual Quantization: A Progressive Multi-Precision Representation for LLMs", Yu Luo, Bo Dong, Wenhua Cheng, Haihao Shen (Intel), arXiv:2608.04048 (Aug 2026): W ≈ base + Σ residual stages; default 2+2+2+2 RTN giving 2/4/6/8-bit prefixes. Explicitly decouples the stages so "the low-bit foundation and the residual stages [can] be constructed with different quantizers" and existing low-bit checkpoints can be reused as the base. Tested on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B/14B, Phi-3-medium; competitive with MatGPTQ at 8 and 6 bits, model-dependent at 4. (2) **Drop-by-Drop**, "Multi-Bitwidth Quantization for LLMs Using Additive Codebooks", Liza Babaoglu, Shuangyi Chen, Ashish Khisti (Toronto), arXiv:2606.12876 (Jun 2026): jointly-optimized additive codebooks with Matryoshka-style supervision over prefixes; dropping a codebook needs **no re-encoding**, only a shorter summation. Theorem 1 proves Gaussian sources are successively refinable under weighted-MSE — the information-theoretic license for multi-precision at no rate penalty. Configs 3×8, 4×8, 5×8 on Gemma-2B, Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen 0.5B–32B. (3) **AnyBCQ**, Gunho Park, Jeongin Bae, Beomseok Kwon et al. (NAVER Cloud), arXiv:2510.10467 (Oct 2025): binary-coded W = Σ αᵢBᵢ; lower-precision binary codes are frozen and later planes capture residual, giving monotonic improvement. Runtime switching is near-free and cheaper than Any-Precision LLM because there is no bit-transpose or centroid lookup. 2-bit MMLU on Llama-3.1-8B 35.32% vs Any-Precision LLM's 24.66%; up to 3.0× vs FP16, 1.2× vs Any-Precision LLM; 49% memory reduction vs separate models. (4) **MoBiQuant**, Dongwei Wang, Jinhee Kim, Seokho Han et al., arXiv:2602.20191 (May 2026): recursive 2-bit slices W_{e+1} residual, reconstruct W^(b) = Σ_{e≤k} W_e for 2/4/6/8-bit; a learned MLP router (MoBiRoute) picks slice count **per token** at runtime, and a single global threshold shift changes the operating point across all layers with no weight repacking. 1.34× throughput over AnyBCQ, 33.8% speedup over Any-Precision LLM, 3.5× memory savings vs separate models.
findings.relevance: This family is the most promising retrofit path for EXL3, because unlike MatQuant it does not require integer MSB structure — the base can be *any* quantizer, including a K2 or K3 trellis code, with cheap RTN/BCQ residual stages layered on top. That would let the trellis base stay untouched (preserving most of EXL3's quality advantage) while the K3→K4 'upgrade' becomes 'materialize one extra residual plane', and the downgrade becomes 'free the plane'. RRQ's explicit claim that stages can use different quantizers and that existing low-bit checkpoints are reusable as the base is exactly the property needed. Also note MoBiQuant's threshold-shift trick: a global scalar knob that trades quality for memory across the whole model instantly, which is a much faster control loop than per-tensor re-encoding and could serve as the emergency/fast path while background re-encoding handles the slow path.

findings.title: EvoPress — proof that per-layer error is NOT monotone or additive, which invalidates naive greedy/knapsack bit allocation
findings.detail: "EvoPress: Accurate Dynamic Model Compression via Evolutionary Search", Oliver Sieberling, Denis Kuznedelev, Eldar Kurtic, Dan Alistarh (IST Austria / ISTA-DASLab), arXiv:2410.14649, ICML 2025. Central claim: existing non-uniform compression methods rest on an unstated assumption that layers contribute *independently and monotonically* to end-to-end error, and this assumption is empirically false — the authors observe that "pruning a model further may even significantly recover performance," i.e. error is non-monotone in the compression level. They therefore replace per-layer-importance heuristics with an evolutionary search over whole compression *profiles* (which layer gets which level), with provable convergence, and apply it uniformly to depth pruning, unstructured sparsity, and per-layer quantization bit-width. SOTA results on Llama, Mistral, Phi across all three compression types. Code at github.com/IST-DASLab/EvoPress.
findings.relevance: This is the strongest methodological warning for the fungible-quant allocator. Every cheap online policy that suggests itself — rank experts by a scalar sensitivity, greedily fill a memory budget, upgrade the top-k — assumes exactly the separability EvoPress shows is wrong. Concretely: upgrading expert A from K3→K4 and expert B from K3→K4 independently may not give the sum of their individual gains, and downgrading a 'safe' expert can interact badly with a previously-downgraded one. Practical implication: an online controller should be conservative (small deltas per interval, validate against a held-out KL probe before committing) rather than trusting an ILP over independently-measured per-tensor error curves. It also argues for keeping a cheap end-to-end verification signal in the loop, which a live serving system is actually *better* positioned to obtain than an offline quantizer.

findings.title: TASA / 'Perplexity Illusion' — PPL-based sensitivity is uncorrelated with reasoning sensitivity, and pure in-domain calibration HURTS
findings.detail: "Beyond Activation Alignment: The Alignment-Diversity Tradeoff in Task-Aware LLM Quantization", Fei Wang, Chao Xue, Taoran Liu, Li Shen, Ye Liu, Changxing Ding (SCUT / JD.com / SYSU / OUC), arXiv:2607.00908 (1 Jul 2026). Two findings. (1) **The Perplexity Illusion**: perplexity-based layer sensitivity has Kendall τ ≈ 0 with reasoning-task sensitivity. PPL-sensitive layers cluster at input embeddings and the output head; reasoning-critical layers sit in the middle of the network. PPL-guided bit allocation therefore *systematically under-protects reasoning*. (2) **The alignment–diversity tradeoff**: calibrating exclusively on target-domain data — maximising activation alignment — actively *degrades* quantization. Pure task data makes the layer-wise Hessian eigenspectrum degenerate (task-relevant eigenvalues blow up, the rest are suppressed), preserving a narrow subspace while destroying broader representational capacity; general-domain data lifts the suppressed eigenvalues and keeps the Hessian well-conditioned. Optimal mixing ratios are model-specific: 50% general for LLaMA-3, 75% for Qwen2.5. Results: at 3.5-bit average, TASA matches 4-bit uniform baselines with 12.5% fewer bits; LLaMA-3-8B GSM8K 46.2% vs 39.4% for uniform W4 — "precision inversion", where task-aware sub-4-bit beats task-agnostic 4-bit.
findings.relevance: This is the sharpest caution against the core premise of workload-specialization. The pitch is 'a quant that starts generic and specializes to each user's actual workload' — this paper says that a quant calibrated *purely* on one workload is worse than one calibrated on a mix, for a concrete spectral reason, and quantifies the right mixing ratio as roughly 50–75% general data. The correct reading is not 'don't specialize' but 'blend': the rolling-window statistics from live serving should be *mixed* with a fixed generic calibration reservoir, not replace it. Separately, the τ≈0 PPL result means the allocation objective must not be perplexity — which is exactly what the KL-based work below argues, and matches llama.cpp practitioner lore (ggml-org/llama.cpp discussion #4110: 'Perplexity, as a quantization loss benchmark, is inaccurate — KL divergence seems to be a better data point').

findings.title: Cheap, calibration-free sensitivity signals — refuting the 'you need BF16 activations on rented B300s' premise
findings.detail: Three separate results give a usable allocation signal without a full-BF16 activation harvest. (1) **AlphaQ**, "Calibration-Free Bit Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Quantization", Wanqi Yang, Yuexiao Ma, Alexander Conzelmann, Xiawu Zheng, Michael W. Mahoney, T. Konstantin Rusch, Shiwei Liu, arXiv:2606.04980 (Jun 2026). Uses Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HT-SR) theory: expert quality is predicted from the *weight spectrum alone* — "experts with more heavy-tailed weight spectra are typically better trained" and get more bits. Solves a budget-constrained error-minimising program with no calibration data at all. Qwen1.5-MoE: near-FP accuracy at 3.5 average bits/expert, 4× compression, beating calibration-based baselines. The paper's explicit motivation is that frontier LLM calibration data is proprietary and "imperfect surrogates misestimate expert utilization." (2) **Router-norm allocation**, "Efficient Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts with Theoretical Generalization Guarantees", Mohammed Nowaz Rabbani Chowdhury, Kaoutar El Maghraoui, Hsinyu Tsai, Naigang Wang, Geoffrey W. Burr, Liu Liu, Meng Wang (RPI / IBM Research), arXiv:2604.06515 (7 Apr 2026). Metric is Λ_s(T) := ‖w_s(T)‖ − ‖w_s(0)‖, the change in each expert's router-vector L2 norm during training (final norm alone as surrogate for pretrained models); experts with *smaller* norm change capture "less frequent but critical features" and get more bits. Cost: "our method only sorts experts by router norm... This requires no GPU and negligible computation." Theorem 4.4 gives a generalization guarantee for the top-κ-fraction-high-bit scheme. Mixtral-8x7B: 68.38% avg accuracy at 2.5 bits vs 62.56% for uniform 2-bit; Switch Transformer holds accuracy to 2.125 avg bits/expert. Notably it **beats activation-frequency and activation-weight baselines**. (3) **Forward-only KL sensitivity**, "A KL Lens on Quantization: Fast, Forward-Only Sensitivity for Mixed-Precision", Kong, Pandey, Ponzina, Rosing (UCSD/SDSU), arXiv:2604.13440 (15 Apr 2026). Per layer: quantize that layer alone, run a calibration forward pass, measure KL(student‖teacher) on logits. Entirely gradient-free — no backprop, no Hessian, no retraining, embarrassingly parallel. Kendall τ 0.79 vs SQNR's 0.76 against ground-truth sensitivity. Mamba-1.4B compressed 7.2× (5.2 GB → 1.4 GB) at negligible PPL loss.
findings.relevance: Directly attacks the stated blocker that deciding bit allocation 'today requires measuring activations with the full BF16 model on rented B300 nodes.' Router-norm needs no GPU at all and is computable from the checkpoint; HT-SR alpha needs only an SVD per expert. Both are also inherently **topology-neutral** — they are properties of the weights/router, not of any TP/DCP sharding — which is the stated requirement. The KL-lens metric is the one most plausibly recomputable *online* in a serving loop: it is one extra forward pass per candidate tensor with the alternate encoding swapped in, which a background worker can do on a spare stream against a rolling sample of real traffic. Important counter-signal though: the RPI/IBM paper found router-norm beats naive activation-frequency ranking, and MoPEQ makes the same point using Hessian trace "instead of relying on the activation frequency of the expert" — so raw hot-expert counts, the most obvious signal from the EPLB-style window, are apparently the *weakest* of the available metrics.

findings.title: MoE expert-level bit allocation as a constrained program — MC-MoE, MoPEQ, BitsMoE, GEMQ
findings.detail: Four MoE-specific allocators, all offline. (1) **MC-MoE**, "Mixture Compressor for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Gains More", Wei Huang, Yue Liao, Jianhui Liu, Ruifei He, Haoru Tan, Shiming Zhang, Hongsheng Li, Si Liu, Xiaojuan Qi, arXiv:2410.06270 (Oct 2024), ICLR 2025. Training-free. Its "Pre-Loading Mixed-Precision Quantization" combines three expert-importance signals — **activation reconstruction error, routing scores, and activated frequencies** — and "formulates the adaptive bit-width allocation as a Linear Programming problem, where the objective function balances multi-factors reflecting the importance of each expert." At 2.54 average bits it compresses 76.6% of the model for 3.8% average accuracy loss; a dynamic-pruning stage further cuts activated params 15% for <0.6% drop. Code: github.com/Aaronhuang-778/MC-MoE. Successor MC# at arXiv:2510.10962. (2) **MoPEQ**, Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata, Jie Ye, Murali Emani (Argonne), arXiv:2509.02512 (Sep 2025): per-expert bit-width from **Hessian trace approximation**, explicitly chosen "instead of relying on the activation frequency of the expert"; 2/3/4-bit on DeepSeek-VL2 tiny/small/base and MolmoE. (3) **BitsMoE**, Jiayu Zhao, Zihan Teng, Minhao Fan, Tianrui Ma, Wentao Ren, Song Chen, Weichen Liu (USTC/NTU), arXiv:2606.00079 (22 May 2026): SVD-decomposes each MoE layer into an FP16 shared basis Φ_h (cross-expert redundancy) plus normalized expert-specific spectral factors; allocates bits to *spectral components* via an ILP with binary y[e,h,k,b], objective min Σ L[e,h,k](b)·y where L = α²·β^γ·E(b), subject to Σ b·y ≤ B_h per projection type and Σ_b y = 1. Bit-width set {16,8,6,4,3,2,1,0} (0 = full eviction), with a piecewise distortion model: η·exp(−λb) for 6–16 bits, empirical κ_b for 2–4 bits, sin²θ angular mismatch at 1 bit. "SVD decomposition and ILP solving contribute only marginally" to overhead — most cost is calibration-statistics collection; 12.3× faster than GPTQ at 2-bit. On Qwen3-30B-A3B at 2-bit: +27.83 points over GPTQ, 1.76× faster decode, 6.29× MoE-layer compression. Also tested on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, Qwen1.5-MoE, Mixtral-8x7B. Code: github.com/zjiayu064/BitsMoE. (4) **GEMQ**, "Global Expert-Level Mixed-Precision Quantization for MoE LLMs", Jianing Deng, Song Wang, Dongwei Wang, Zijie Liu, Tianlong Chen, Huanrui Yang, Jingtong Hu, arXiv:2605.23078 (May 2026): a *global* (cross-layer, not per-layer) expert importance metric incorporating routing frequency and activation statistics.
findings.relevance: These are the closest offline analogues of what the online controller would have to solve each interval, and they establish the right shape of the program: binary assignment variables per (expert, bit-width), a linear bit-budget constraint, exactness constraint, and a distortion model E(b) fitted per tensor. BitsMoE is the most directly reusable — its piecewise distortion model η·exp(−λb) for high bits and empirical κ_b for low bits is exactly the error-vs-bpw curve a runtime allocator needs to cache per tensor, and the ILP is reported as cheap to solve (the expensive part is statistics collection, which a live server gets for free). GEMQ's *global* framing also matters: allocating within a layer's expert set is much weaker than allocating across all 256×N experts model-wide, and a global budget is what a memory-constrained 4×96 GB box actually has. Caution: all four are offline, and all four assume separable per-expert error, which EvoPress disputes.

findings.title: The HAWQ lineage — the origin of Hessian-based mixed precision, and HAWQ-V3's ILP under multi-resource constraints
findings.detail: (1) **HAWQ**, Zhen Dong, Zhewei Yao, Amir Gholami, Michael Mahoney, Kurt Keutzer, arXiv:1905.03696 (ICCV 2019): selects each layer's relative precision from the *top Hessian eigenvalue* of that layer's block, and derives a deterministic fine-tuning order from the same second-order information. Motivation stated exactly as the problem here: "there is no systematic way to determine the precision of different layers... the search space for mixed-precision is exponential in the number of layers." (2) **HAWQ-V2**, arXiv:1911.03852 (NeurIPS 2020): replaces the top eigenvalue with the **average Hessian trace** as the sensitivity measure, and shows the top eigenvalue alone is a poor proxy. (3) **HAWQ-V3**, Zhewei Yao et al., arXiv:2011.10680 (ICML 2021 spotlight): integer-only dyadic arithmetic plus a **hardware-aware Integer Linear Program** that minimises total model perturbation Σ Ω_i subject to *simultaneous* constraints on model size, latency, and total bit-operations — the first clean statement of bit allocation as a multi-resource-constrained ILP. ResNet50 INT8 77.58%; mixed INT4/8 cuts INT8 latency 23% at 76.73%. (4) **Q-BERT**, Sheng Shen, Zhen Dong et al., arXiv:1909.05840 (AAAI 2020): brings this to transformers with group-wise quantization; layers with flatter Hessian curvature go to lower precision; down to 2 bits with ≤2.3% degradation, 13× weight compression.
findings.relevance: This is the conceptual ancestor of everything else here and supplies the vocabulary — 'sensitivity Ω_i', 'perturbation budget', 'ILP under a size constraint' — that the fungible-quant design document should use. HAWQ-V3's multi-resource ILP is the right template because the real constraint set here is not just bytes: it is per-GPU VRAM under TP4 (not aggregate), plus decode bandwidth, plus whatever the DCP4 KV budget needs. The V1→V2 progression (top eigenvalue → trace) is also a useful warning that the first plausible scalar sensitivity metric was wrong.

findings.title: Non-MoE LLM allocators as constrained optimization — LLM-MQ, MixQuant, GAMMA, CMPQ, VBQ
findings.detail: (1) **LLM-MQ** (NICS-EFC, Tsinghua; NeurIPS'23 ENLSP workshop): layer-wise precision over {2,3,4} bits under a target memory budget, sensitivity from a **first-order Taylor approximation** of output loss, solved as an integer program minimising the weighted sum of per-layer sensitivities subject to the memory constraint; plus sparse outlier protection keeping 0.5% of weights in FP16 as CSR with the remaining outliers at INT2. (2) **MixQuant**, arXiv:2607.23047: casts bit allocation as a **multiple-choice knapsack problem** and solves it greedily. (3) **GAMMA**, "Global Bit Allocation for Mixed-Precision Models under Arbitrary Budgets", Zhangyang Yao, Haiyan Zhao, Haoyu Wang, Tianbo Huang, Lihua Zhang, Xu Han (Beihang / Tsinghua / ByteDance), arXiv:2605.18475 (18 May 2026): two-stage — Stage I learns module-wise precision *preferences* by differentiable relaxation (Gumbel-Softmax masks over bit choices) against a teacher-forced layer-wise hidden-state reconstruction loss with an augmented-Lagrangian budget term, no weight retraining; Stage II projects the soft preferences into an exactly-budget-feasible discrete assignment via a knapsack-style ILP/DP. Granularity is the linear module (q/k/v/FFN) inside each transformer layer. Llama3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B/14B/32B; matches 3-bit quality at 2.5-bit average; up to +12.99 average points over fixed-precision and search-based baselines. (4) **CMPQ**, "Channel-Wise Mixed-Precision Quantization for Large Language Models" / "Adapting to Any Bit-Width", Zihan Chen, Bike Xie, Jundong Li, Cong Shen, arXiv:2410.13056 (Oct 2024): per-*channel* bit-widths from activation distributions, non-uniform quantization plus two outlier-extraction techniques, explicitly supporting **arbitrary non-integer average bit-widths between 2 and 4** — most prior work only hits integer bits. Nine LLMs. (5) **VBQ**, Hamish Ogilvy, arXiv:2607.02893 (3 Jul 2026): per-*group* (64 contiguous weights) learned precision over {1,2,4,8} via Gumbel-Softmax with gradient isolation and alternating weight/precision updates; the discovered recipe is stable enough to freeze (69% of groups collapse to 1 bit, first MLP block keeps ~2.5 bits); fused dequant-matmul kernels give ~1.86× at 1.0B and ~4.68× at 99B on Apple silicon; a 131M model at 1.82 mean bits beats a 55M FP16 baseline at 3.8× less storage. (6) **Scaling Laws For Mixed Quantization**, Zeyu Cao et al., arXiv:2410.06722: defines quantization ratio Q_r (fraction of params at low precision) and block size Q_b; finds larger models tolerate higher Q_r at fixed quality, and finer granularity permits higher Q_r.
findings.relevance: Together these fix the design space for the allocator: granularity (layer < module < expert < channel < 64-weight group), sensitivity source (Taylor first-order / Hessian trace / learned Gumbel preference / activation distribution), and solver (greedy multiple-choice knapsack → DP → ILP). CMPQ matters specifically because arbitrary fractional average bpw is exactly what a K3/K4 mix produces and most of the literature only handles integer bits. GAMMA's two-stage 'learn soft preference, then project onto an exactly-feasible discrete point' is a good pattern for an online controller — the soft preference can be updated incrementally from streaming statistics while the projection step enforces the hard VRAM budget at each rebalance. VBQ's finding that the learned allocation 'stabilizes early enough to freeze into a fixed recipe' is a caution: it suggests allocation may converge quickly and that continuous re-optimization buys less than expected. The scaling-law result (bigger models tolerate more low-precision; finer granularity helps) is favourable for a 256-expert MoE at expert granularity.

findings.title: Outlier-aware mixed precision — OWQ, SpQR, AWQ, and the GPTQ/OBQ error framing every allocator inherits
findings.detail: (1) **GPTQ**, Elias Frantar, Saleh Ashkboos, Torsten Hoefler, Dan Alistarh, arXiv:2210.17323 (ICLR 2023), building on **Optimal Brain Compression / OBQ**, arXiv:2208.11580 (NeurIPS 2022). GPTQ does *not* allocate bits — it fixes the bit-width and minimises the layer-wise proxy ‖WX − ŴX‖²_F using approximate second-order (Hessian ≈ 2XXᵀ from calibration activations) error compensation, quantizing 175B params in ~4 GPU-hours at 3–4 bits. Its contribution to allocation is the *objective*: essentially every subsequent allocator consumes GPTQ-style per-tensor reconstruction error as its E(b) curve. (2) **OWQ**, Changhun Lee, Jungyu Jin, Taesu Kim, Hyungjun Kim, Eunhyeok Park, arXiv:2306.02272, **AAAI 2024 oral**: identifies a small set of *structured* (column-level) weights made sensitive by activation outliers and keeps them in high precision while quantizing the dense remainder hard — 3.01-bit OWQ ≈ 4-bit OPTQ quality. Mixed precision at *column* granularity, decided offline from calibration activations. (3) **SpQR**, Tim Dettmers, Ruslan Svirschevski, Vage Egiazarian, Denis Kuznedelev, Elias Frantar, Saleh Ashkboos, Alexander Borzunov, Torsten Hoefler, Dan Alistarh, arXiv:2306.03078 (ICLR 2024): isolates individual outlier weights causing large error into a 16-bit sparse side-channel, everything else at 3–4 bits, with small groups and quantized second-level scales; first near-lossless compression at those rates. (4) **AWQ**, Ji Lin, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, Xingyu Dang, Song Han, arXiv:2306.00978, **MLSys 2024 best paper**: no bit allocation at all — instead observes that ~1% of weight *channels* are salient, identifies them **from the activation distribution, not the weight magnitude**, and protects them by an equivalent per-channel scaling transform. Notably, "AWQ does not rely on any backpropagation or reconstruction, so it generalizes to different domains and modalities without overfitting the calibration set," and its scales are collected offline from activation statistics. (5) **SqueezeLLM**, Sehoon Kim, Coleman Hooper, Amir Gholami, Zhen Dong, Xiuyu Li, Sheng Shen, Michael Mahoney, Kurt Keutzer, arXiv:2306.07629 (ICML 2024) — **important correction to the framing in the brief**: SqueezeLLM's 'sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization' varies the *placement of quantization levels*, not the number of bits per layer. It solves a Fisher-weighted k-means, min_C Σ_i h_i ‖w_i − c_{q(w_i)}‖², where h_i is the Fisher/Hessian-diagonal sensitivity of weight i — fixed bit-width, non-uniform centroids — combined with Dense-and-Sparse decomposition holding outliers and sensitive values in a sparse FP16 side matrix. 3-bit closes the PPL gap to FP16 by up to 2.1× vs prior SOTA on LLaMA.
findings.relevance: Three things matter here. First, the precise correction on SqueezeLLM: it is a non-uniform-*level* method, not a per-layer bit-allocator — worth getting right in any design doc, and it is also the exact backbone Any-Precision LLM needed for nesting (uniform quantizers like AWQ break under incremental upscaling). Second, OWQ and SpQR show that the highest-leverage mixed precision is often at *sub-tensor* granularity (columns, individual outliers) rather than whole experts — protecting 0.5–1% of weights buys roughly a full bit. For a K3 MoE that suggests a cheaper knob than K3→K4 wholesale: attach a small FP16 outlier side-channel to hot experts, which is additive, size-predictable, and hot-swappable without touching the trellis payload at all. Third, AWQ's claim that activation-magnitude salience generalizes across domains *without overfitting the calibration set* is the strongest published argument that workload-specific re-allocation may buy less than hoped — it directly contradicts the premise that per-user specialization is where the wins are.

findings.title: Other runtime/elastic precision systems — DyMoE, FlexQuant, Context-Aware MoE on CXL-NDP, QPART
findings.detail: (1) **DyMoE**, "Dynamic Expert Orchestration with Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient MoE Inference on Edge", Yuegui Huang, Zhiyuan Fang, Weiqi Luo, Ruoyu Wu, Wuhui Chen, Zibin Zheng, arXiv:2603.19172 (19 Mar 2026). Phase-adaptive importance: during *prefill* it aggregates attention weights across heads to find heavy-hitter tokens and prioritises the experts serving them; during *decode* it uses gating scores directly. A depth-aware cosine schedule gives more high-precision experts to early layers. Critically it does **not re-quantize online** — experts are pre-quantized offline with GPTQ into 4-bit and 2-bit versions, and the runtime cache keeps only *one* copy per expert, loading the appropriate version on demand. Mixtral-8x7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B under 12–24 GB; 3.44–22.7× TTFT and up to 14.58× TPOT speedup. (2) **FlexQuant**, Yuji Chai, Mujin Kwen, David Brooks, Gu-Yeon Wei (Harvard), arXiv:2501.07139 (13 Jan 2025): generates an *ensemble* of quantized models for elastic hosting under a fluctuating unified memory pool; bits can be truncated or re-appended at runtime with total storage set only by the largest precision; claims 15× granularity improvement and 10× storage reduction vs prior multi-model hosting. (3) **Context-Aware Mixture-of-Experts Inference on CXL-Enabled GPU-NDP Systems**, arXiv:2512.04476: uses *prefill-stage* activation statistics to guide decode-stage expert placement, pins hot experts in HBM and maps the rest to CXL near-data-processing, with context-aware per-expert bitwidths of 1–4 bits. Explicitly describes hot→warm→cold transitions triggered by sustained below-threshold selection frequency with a **hysteresis window to avoid thrashing**, run asynchronously on a separate stream "with no blocking synchronization step on the inference path." (4) **QPART**, arXiv:2506.23934: server dynamically ships a quantized model and adaptively shares inference workload with the device, accuracy-aware.
findings.relevance: Rounds out the picture that runtime per-expert precision management is now a small but real subfield with converged engineering answers: pre-quantize offline into a small set of levels, keep hotness statistics with EMA + hysteresis, move on a side CUDA stream, never re-encode on the critical path. DyMoE's 'store one copy, pick the version' and the CXL paper's explicit hysteresis-on-selection-frequency both reinforce DynaExq's design. Notably *none* of them re-encodes online — which is the one part of the fungible-quant proposal that has no published precedent, and the part whose cost (Hessian collection + Viterbi trellis search per tensor) is the real open question.

findings.title: vLLM EPLB in this tree: the same-shape assumption is explicit in code, and the statistics window is already there to reuse
findings.detail:
The size asymmetry noted in the brief is not merely implicit — it is an explicit code comment. In /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/distributed/eplb/rebalance_execute.py, `rearrange_expert_weights_inplace` (line 550) allocates its exchange buffers at lines 605-610 as:

    # NOTE: Currently we assume the same weights across different layers
    # have the same shape.
    weights_buffer: list[torch.Tensor] = [
        torch.empty_like(w) for w in first_layer_weights
    ]

Every transfer is then a same-shape `copy_` (lines 251, 427, 465) into that `empty_like` buffer, and shapes are asserted equal at lines 184, 529, 592, 599. So a bit-width change is structurally incompatible with this path. Conversely, the *statistics* half of EPLB is directly reusable: /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/distributed/eplb/eplb_state.py already maintains `expert_load_pass` (line 148) accumulated per step and folded into `expert_load_window` of shape (window_size, num_moe_layers, num_physical_experts) (lines 155-159, 448-456), advanced in `step()` (line 517) with a circular `expert_load_window_step` (lines 604-611) and an all-reduce in `_sync_load_pass`, plus `async_worker.py` for off-critical-path rebalancing.
findings.relevance: Concretely scopes the vLLM work. The statistics layer needed for a fungible-quant controller — rolling per-expert activation counts, windowed, EP-synchronised, with an existing async worker to run the policy off the critical path — is already built and tested and could be extended rather than written. What must be new is the *execution* layer: `rearrange_expert_weights_inplace` cannot be reused at all for a bit-width change, and the two published answers are MorphServe's (write the smaller tensor into the pre-reserved larger slot, pointer never moves, pay internal fragmentation) or DynaExq's (pointer indirection behind a stable handle + two size-homogeneous fixed-block pools, pay a second resident copy). Also note the EPLB window is keyed on *physical* experts, so under EP it is topology-dependent; since EP is not used here (TP4+DCP4, DP=1) the counts are naturally logical and therefore already topology-neutral, which is convenient for the stated requirement.

findings.title: Survey anchor for the whole subfield
findings.detail: "Mixed-Precision Quantization for Language Models: Techniques and Prospects", Mariam Rakka, Marios Fournarakis, Olga Krestinskaya, Jinane Bazzi, Khaled N. Salama, Fadi Kurdahi, Ahmed M. Eltawil, Mohammed E. Fouda, arXiv:2510.16805 (19 Oct 2025), 46 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Categorises and compares recent mixed-precision LM frameworks "according to their bit allocation strategies and precision configurations across weights, activations, and key-value caches," and closes on open issues including hardware-aware design, activation quantization, and scalable optimization methods for billion-parameter models. Complementary older survey for the CNN-era foundations: "Mixed-Precision Neural Networks: A Survey", arXiv:2208.06064.
findings.relevance: The right single citation to anchor a design document's related-work section, and the fastest way to check whether anything in the offline-allocation space has been missed. Its own stated open problems (hardware-aware design, scalable optimization) are precisely where the fungible-quant idea would have to claim novelty — note that neither the 2025 survey's open-problems list nor its taxonomy appears to include *online/serving-time re-allocation*, which is consistent with DynaExq (Nov 2025) being roughly the first entry in that category.

gaps: No published work on online/runtime bit-width reallocation for TRELLIS-coded (QTIP/EXL3/exllamav3) weights specifically. Every runtime system found (DynaExq, MorphServe, DyMoE, CXL-MoE) uses INT2/3/4/8 or FP16 with GPTQ/RTN-style codecs. The cost of a background Viterbi re-encode of a single expert tensor on an SM120 GPU — the central feasibility number for the re-encode variant of the proposal — is unmeasured anywhere in the literature and would have to be benchmarked directly.

Could not recover exllamav3's actual per-tensor/per-expert bitrate allocation algorithm. The docs explicitly defer to the source ("A full description of the format is coming, but until then I refer to the code"), the DeepWiki page does not cover it, and a GitHub code search over turboderp-org/exllamav3 for bitrate/bits_per_weight returned only exllamav3/conversion/quant_config.py (`bits_per_weight = shape[-1] // 16`). Whether EXL3 picks mixed bitrates by measured error curve, a knapsack, or a hand-tuned heuristic is unresolved without reading the quantizer source locally.

No paper found on TOPOLOGY-NEUTRAL bit allocation as an explicit requirement. HAWQ-V3 has hardware-aware constraints but they are fixed at quantization time; nothing addresses making an allocation valid across arbitrary TP/PP/DCP splits or GPU counts. Relatedly, no runtime-precision system found operates under tensor parallelism at all — DynaExq is single-GPU, MorphServe's swap analysis is single-replica, DyMoE is edge/single-device. How a per-expert precision map interacts with TP4 sharding of the expert weight matrices (does a 'K4 expert' mean all four shards go to K4?) is entirely unaddressed.

No study quantifies how much a good bit allocation actually DRIFTS with workload over time, which is the load-bearing empirical assumption of the whole idea. DynaExq assumes routing drifts but measures accuracy/throughput, not the stability of the allocation decision itself. Counter-evidence exists in both directions and is unresolved: VBQ (arXiv:2607.02893) found the learned allocation 'stabilizes early enough to freeze into a fixed recipe', and AWQ claims activation-based salience generalizes across domains without calibration overfitting — both suggest the allocation may converge and stop moving, in which case a one-time warmup specialization would capture most of the value and the continuous re-balancing machinery would be wasted.

No cost/benefit analysis anywhere of re-encoding versus storing multiple bit-width copies at MoE scale. For 256 experts × N layers, the disk/host-RAM cost of keeping both K3 and K4 encodings resident versus the compute cost of background re-encoding is exactly the tradeoff the design turns on, and no paper models it.

Could not retrieve the detailed taxonomy, per-category citation table, or open-problems list of the main survey (arXiv:2510.16805) — only its abstract was accessible via fetch. The claim that it omits online reallocation is inferred from the abstract's open-issues sentence, not verified against the body.

Nothing found on bit allocation for MTP / speculative-decoding DRAFT layers specifically — i.e. whether the right sensitivity objective for a draft head is acceptance length rather than KL or PPL, and how bits should be split between the draft layer and the target model under a shared budget. The collector work described in the brief appears to be ahead of the published literature here.

No academic treatment of quantizing dense/attention layers ONLINE at startup and caching (the K6/MXFP8-at-startup part of the proposal). The literature treats quantization as a separate offline pipeline stage; startup-time quantization inside the serving engine appears only incidentally (EXL3 mentions on-the-fly Hessians and single-step conversion) and is not studied as a system design.

summary: Yes — the core idea has been built, and recently. DynaExq (arXiv 2511.15015, Nov 2025, UConn/UCSC) is a near-exact precedent: it estimates long-horizon expert "hotness" from router traces via EMA, selects a per-layer high-precision resident set with a budget-feasible top-n rule under a fixed HBM envelope, and applies asynchronous promotions/demotions through "stable expert handles" — hot experts get more bits, cold experts fewer, decided online. HOBBIT (arXiv 2411.01433) and its ASPLOS'26 successor MoE-APEX do mixed-precision expert serving at per-token granularity, and MC-MoE/MxMoE/GEMQ/AlphaQ solve the offline "which expert deserves which bits" problem with LP solvers costing ~1 second. Critically, NO system re-quantizes online: every one of them stores pre-quantized copies at each precision and swaps them, and DynaExq specifically dodges the tensor-size-change problem with two separate fixed-size-block HBM pools (one per format) plus a CPU-side index and reclaim-after-register — never a fixed-shape in-place copy. The empirical crux is genuinely mixed: skew within a request is severe (MoE-Infinity: one expert reused 7x more than any other; <5% of experts repeatedly activated per request), but MoE-Infinity also measured that "reuse counts even out over time" across 1000+ sequences, i.e. the model-level histogram flattens — and Mixtral shows no topic specialization while OLMoE (from-scratch, fine-grained) shows strong domain specialization, so stability is model- and workload-homogeneity-dependent. The biggest unexplored territory for the GG stack is exactly where its constraints bite: nothing does this under tensor parallelism, nothing does online re-encoding from BF16, nothing uses trellis/EXL3 codes (which are not bit-nested, so MatQuant-style slicing doesn't transfer), and vLLM's own RFC #30359 states CUDA graph data pointers cannot be updated after capture — a bit-width change alters tensor byte size, so it cannot be copied into the captured buffer.

findings.title: DynaExq — the direct precedent: online hot/cold expert precision promotion under a memory budget
findings.detail: Kexin Chu, Dawei Xiang, Zixu Shen, Yiwei Yang, Zecheng Lin, Wei Zhang. "Dynamic Expert Quantization for Scalable Mixture-of-Experts Inference" (DynaExq), arXiv:2511.15015v1, 19 Nov 2025 (Univ. of Connecticut / UC Santa Cruz). Hotness = EMA of router probabilities, S_i(t) = alpha*S_i(t-1) + (1-alpha)*g_i(x_t), updated on a coarse period T (neither alpha nor T disclosed). Allocation is a 'budget-feasible top-n rule': solve n_hot*S_hot + n_cold*S_cold <= M_HBM with n_hot + n_cold = N, sort experts by S_i, promote the top n_hot. Two precision tiers only; evaluated FP16-vs-INT4 (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and INT4-vs-INT2 (Qwen3-80B-A3B); all router/non-expert components stay full precision. Results: 73.09% -> 77.57% accuracy on Qwen3-80B, up to 2.73x throughput over offload/prefetch baselines at batch 32, on single RTX 5090 and A6000. Six benchmarks (WikiText-2, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, AIME25, GSM8K, HumanEval, MMLU-ProX).
findings.relevance: This is the answer to 'has anyone already built it': yes, ten months ago, and the architecture is a one-for-one match to the proposal (rolling activation window -> periodic budget-constrained precision decision -> async background swap -> atomic handoff). The user should treat this as prior art to cite and to differentiate against, not as a reason to abandon: DynaExq is single-GPU only (future work explicitly lists 'integrating DynaExq into distributed MoE serving frameworks'), has only 2 tiers, and never re-encodes — all three are exactly where the GG stack's TP4+DCP4 / K2-K3-K4 / online-EXL3 design would be novel.

findings.title: DynaExq's answer to the CRITICAL ASYMMETRY: two format-segregated fixed-block pools, not a fixed-shape in-place copy
findings.detail: DynaExq does NOT do an EPLB-style same-shape swap. Verbatim from the paper: 'DynaExq partitions HBM into two dedicated pools for high- and low-precision experts. Each pool is subdivided into fixed-size blocks aligned with the corresponding data format.' A compact CPU-side index records expert locations and pool occupancy; runtime cudaMalloc is avoided entirely to eliminate allocator-induced jitter. On a transition it 'immediately reclaims the old representation once the new weight is successfully registered, ensuring that no expert holds dual copies longer than necessary,' and 'a small transient buffer absorbs transfer bursts, allowing multiple in-flight promotions without exceeding the memory budget.' During a promotion in flight, 'DynaExq always uses the last stable version of each expert' — the forward pass never sees a partially materialized tensor. Transfers go SSD -> DRAM -> HBM on dedicated CUDA streams.
findings.relevance: This directly resolves the concern that 'a fixed-shape in-place copy is not sufficient.' The trick is per-format block pools sized to the format, so within a pool every block IS the same size — the size change is absorbed by moving between pools rather than resizing a tensor. It also answers the fragmentation and atomic-swap-reserve concerns: reserve is bounded to one transient burst buffer, fragmentation is structurally prevented by fixed blocks. This is a directly transplantable design for the GG K2/K3/K4 case (three pools instead of two).

findings.title: NOBODY re-quantizes online — every system swaps pre-quantized copies, which is the single clearest novelty gap
findings.detail: DynaExq: 'High-precision and low-precision weights are stored on SSD and cached in DRAM, and all transfers to HBM use dedicated CUDA streams' — pre-computed, not re-encoded. HOBBIT: 'we use int4 precision versions as replacements for the float16 precision models and int2 versions for the int8 precision models', with both variants resident in CPU memory. Mixtral-offloading (Eliseev & Mazur, github.com/dvmazur/mixtral-offloading): HQQ 4-bit attention + 2-bit experts, fixed at build time, LRU cache over experts. FlexQuant (arXiv:2506.12024): 'models with different accuracies can be saved in inexpensive storage and prefetching the next round of switching to weights into the HBM is performed by GPU-Direct' — INT8 and INT4 copies both stored; switching order determined OFFLINE by KL divergence ranking; switch decisions every 20 generated tokens via a sliding-window perplexity-entropy (PPLE) threshold; dense models only, no MoE.
findings.relevance: The proposal's step 3 — 'RE-ENCODE the new bit-width weights asynchronously in the background' — is unprecedented. Everyone else pays 2x storage (cheap, on SSD) to avoid encode cost. For EXL3/trellis this matters a lot: Viterbi trellis search is far more expensive than an INT4 round-to-nearest, so background re-encoding may be minutes not milliseconds. The pragmatic path with strong precedent is: keep K2/K3/K4 EXL3 artifacts for every expert on NVMe (built once at startup or fetched from HF), and make the runtime job pure paging, not encoding. That collapses 'slow reaction time' from an encode problem to a PCIe bandwidth problem.

findings.title: HOBBIT / MoE-APEX — mixed-precision expert offloading with per-TOKEN precision choice, verified in detail
findings.detail: Peng Tang, Jiacheng Liu, Xiaofeng Hou, Yifei Pu, Jing Wang, Pheng-Ann Heng, Chao Li, Minyi Guo (SJTU + CUHK). HOBBIT: arXiv:2411.01433v2, Nov 2024. Journal/conference version: 'MoE-APEX: An Efficient MoE Inference System with Adaptive Precision Expert Offloading', ASPLOS 2026, DOI 10.1145/3779212.3790187. Confirmed mixed-precision mechanism: precision pairs are FP16+INT4 (RTX 4090) and INT8+INT2 (Jetson Orin). Criticality is a CUMULATIVE GATING MAGNITUDE, Eq. 2: s_{e_i}(x) = sum_{j=0}^{i-1} ||G(x)_{e_j}||, i.e. the running sum of L2 gate norms over the token's top-K experts ranked by weight; thresholds T1=0.6 and T2=0.9 (Mixtral) partition into high-precision / low-precision / skip, and 'the first expert (e_0) is always treated as important, keeping it in high precision.' Precision is chosen PER TOKEN at runtime, and only for cache MISSES. Layer-level adaptive prefetch exploits 'strong layer-wise similarity of gating inputs' — 96% next-layer expert prediction accuracy. Sequence-level cache is a weighted 4-term score (Eq. 3): p_t = w_lru*LRU + w_lfu*LFU + w_lhu*LHU + w_fld*FLD, where LHU ('last high-precision use') counts only high-precision usage and FLD is distance from the current layer. Up to 9.93x decode speedup over SOTA MoE offloading, implemented on llama.cpp.
findings.relevance: HOBBIT is the closest thing to 'mixed-precision expert caching' and confirms the reported claim. But note the crucial semantic difference from the proposal: HOBBIT uses low precision as a LATENCY HEDGE on a cache miss (fetch fewer bytes now), not as a persistent memory-budget allocation. The user's idea and DynaExq's are the residency-allocation framing. HOBBIT's LHU metric is nevertheless directly reusable: tracking 'how often was this expert needed AT high precision' is a better promotion signal than raw frequency, and the cumulative-gate-norm criticality score is a cheap, topology-neutral per-expert importance signal computable from router outputs the collector plugin already captures.

findings.title: MC-MoE — the canonical offline solver for 'which expert deserves the bits', and it costs ~1 second
findings.detail: 'MC-MoE: Mixture Compressor for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Gains More', arXiv:2410.06270, Oct 2024 (HKU / CUHK / Beihang), ICLR/OpenReview id xAc3bkVblw. Pre-Loading Mixed-Precision Quantization (PMQ) formulates per-expert bit allocation from {1,2,3} bits as a Linear Program (non-expert components uniformly 4-bit). Objective: minimize sum_i sum_{j=1..3} phi_i^alpha * w_i^beta * (eps_{i,j} * x_{i,j})^gamma, where phi_i = expert access frequency (activations / dataset size), w_i = summed routing weights (activation-weighted importance), eps_{i,j} = Frobenius-norm reconstruction error of expert i at j bits, and alpha/beta/gamma are balancing hyperparameters. 'The solution takes approximately one second to compute.' Results: 2.54 bpw -> 67.50% avg accuracy (3.8% loss vs FP16); 1.57 bpw -> 54.49% (16.8% loss); 96.80 GB -> 10.82-16.65 GB. Also has Online Dynamic Pruning (ODP) that drops experts for unimportant tokens at inference.
findings.relevance: This is the concrete recipe for the part the user calls 'the hard, unsolved part' — and it is neither unsolved nor expensive. All three LP inputs are obtainable on the user's own hardware: phi_i and w_i come straight from router traces (the glm52-mtp78-collector already captures exactly this: top-8 IDs plus gate values over 7.3M live tokens), and eps_{i,j} is a pure weight-space quantity — the Frobenius error of quantizing expert i to j bits — computable locally with no B300 rental and no full-BF16 forward pass. The LP's 1-second solve time also means the decision step is essentially free to re-run every EPLB-style interval, making the online version tractable.

findings.title: AlphaQ — calibration-free per-expert bit allocation from weight spectra, kills the 'need a B300 node' premise
findings.detail: 'AlphaQ: Calibration-Free Bit Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Quantization', arXiv:2606.04980, submitted 3 June 2026. Uses Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HT-SR) theory to measure per-expert 'spectral heavy-tailedness' (the power-law exponent of each expert weight matrix's eigenspectrum) as a proxy for training quality / information content. Experts with stronger heavy-tailed spectral structure get more bits. Solves 'a budget-constrained optimization problem that minimizes total quantization error under a global bit-budget constraint.' Results: Qwen1.5-MoE at an average expert precision of only 3.5 bits reaches near-full-precision accuracy with >4x memory compression, and the paper claims it consistently OUTPERFORMS calibration-based methods — arguing frontier LLM training distributions are proprietary so calibration data is unrepresentative anyway. Code on GitHub. Evaluated across DeepSeek, Qwen-MoE, Mixtral.
findings.relevance: Directly contradicts the stated blocker that deciding bit allocation 'today requires measuring activations with the full BF16 model on rented B300 nodes.' AlphaQ needs only the weights. It is also inherently topology-neutral — a per-expert eigenspectrum exponent has no dependence on TP degree or GPU count, so the allocation transfers across TP4/TP2/TP8 unchanged. The strongest practical design is likely a hybrid: AlphaQ-style spectral alpha as the static prior (available at startup with zero calibration), MC-MoE-style phi/w from live router traces as the online correction term.

findings.title: MxMoE — mixed-precision expert allocation WITH mixed-precision GroupGEMM kernel co-design
findings.detail: Haojie Duanmu, Xiuhong Li, Zhihang Yuan et al., 'MxMoE: Mixed-precision Quantization for MoE with Accuracy and Performance Co-Design', arXiv:2505.05799, 9 May 2025. Two signals drive allocation: (1) parameter sensitivity — different linear blocks have different quantization sensitivity; (2) expert activation dynamics — experts have divergent activation frequencies creating heterogeneous compute characteristics. Its distinguishing contribution is systems-side: it 'automatically generates optimized mixed-precision GroupGEMM kernels, enabling parallel execution of GEMMs with different precisions.' Results: 2.4x lower perplexity than GPTQ at 2.25-bit; up to 3.4x speedup over FP; 29.4% faster than uniform 5-bit at matched accuracy. Allocation is offline.
findings.relevance: This is the piece of the puzzle SparkInfer would have to own. Once experts within a single fused-MoE layer carry different bit-widths (K2/K3/K4 mixed), the grouped GEMM has to dispatch heterogeneous-precision tiles in one launch or the throughput win evaporates. MxMoE is the existence proof that it can be autogenerated and is worth 29.4% over uniform at equal accuracy — but on SM120 with CuTe DSL and EXL3 trellis tiles (16x16, Tensor-Core-aligned) this kernel work is bespoke and is probably the largest engineering line item after the swap machinery.

findings.title: GEMQ and MODE — 2026 state of the art in expert-level mixed precision: global LP plus router repair
findings.detail: GEMQ: Jianing Deng, Song Wang, Dongwei Wang, Zijie Liu, Tianlong Chen, Huanrui Yang, Jingtong Hu, 'Global Expert-level Mixed-precision Quantization for MoE LLMs', arXiv:2605.23078, 21 May 2026. Abstract verbatim: existing methods 'rely on layer-wise importance estimation and overlook router shifts induced by quantization, resulting in suboptimal allocation and routing.' GEMQ contributes (1) a GLOBAL (model-wide, not per-layer) linear-programming formulation of expert importance grounded in quantization error analysis, and (2) efficient router fine-tuning to adapt routing to already-quantized experts, integrated in a progressive framework that iteratively refines importance estimation and allocation. MODE: 'Modality-Decomposed Expert-Level Mixed-Precision Quantization for MoE Multimodal LLMs', arXiv:2606.17118, June 2026 — modality-affinity-aware Hessian objective based on token-expert affinity.
findings.relevance: Two takeaways for the design. First, GEMQ shows layer-local bit budgets are leaving accuracy on the table — the budget should be solved GLOBALLY across all 256 experts x all layers, which fits the proposal's 'fixed memory budget' framing well. Second, and more important: 'router shifts induced by quantization' is called out as a first-class failure mode, and GEMQ's fix is to fine-tune the router after allocation. In an ONLINE rebalancing loop that becomes a moving target — every promotion/demotion perturbs routing, which perturbs the hotness statistics that drove the decision. The iterative/progressive structure GEMQ uses offline is the right mental model for damping that loop online.

findings.title: The routing-consistency cluster (EAQuant, MoEQuant, ExpertQuant, EAC-MoE) — quantization moves the router, and that is the dominant error term
findings.detail: Four independent groups converge on the same conclusion. EAQuant (arXiv:2506.13329, June 2025; code at github.com/darren-fzq1/EAQuant): three expert-aware mechanisms — smoothing aggregation for activation outliers, ROUTING CONSISTENCY ALIGNMENT to preserve expert selection post-quantization, and calibration data balance for sparsely activated experts; validated at W4A4/W3A4/W3A3/W2A4. MoEQuant (Xing Hu et al., arXiv:2505.03804, May 2025): identifies inter-expert imbalance (uneven calibration samples per expert -> biased calibration for rare experts) and intra-expert imbalance; fixes with Expert-Balanced Sampling + Affinity Guidance. 'Router Choice Matters: Rank-Aware Post-Training Quantization for MoE Models' / ExpertQuant (OpenReview kPgLp47bJf, ICML 2026 workshop): shows 'router errors cascade into expert selection and dominate accuracy loss' and that 'most errors arise as near-neighbor rank flips around the top-k experts'; introduces Rank-Aware Jaccard Loss (aligns top-k rank) and Gap Hinge Loss (preserves score margins between consecutive experts); evaluated on OLMoE, DeepSeek-MoE, Qwen3-MoE at W4A8. EAC-MoE (Chen, Shao, Wang, Cheng, ACL 2025 Long, arXiv:2508.01625): Quantization with Expert-Selection Calibration (QESC) recalibrates the routers themselves post-quantization; Pruning based on Expert-Selection Frequency (PESF) prunes rarely-used experts 'for current task'.
findings.relevance: This is the sharpest technical risk to the online-rebalancing loop and none of the runtime systems (DynaExq, HOBBIT) address it. The feedback path is: change expert i's bit-width -> its output changes -> downstream router logits change -> top-8 membership flips for tokens near the k-th margin -> measured hotness changes -> the policy promotes/demotes different experts next window. With top-8 out of 256 and fine-grained experts, the margins between the 8th and 9th expert are thin, so rank flips are likely. Mitigations with precedent: use Gap Hinge / margin-preservation when quantizing (ExpertQuant), add hysteresis/dead-bands to promotion thresholds beyond DynaExq's EMA, pin the router itself at BF16 (DynaExq keeps 'all non-expert and routing components in full precision'), and measure top-8 Jaccard overlap before and after each swap as a rollback guard.

findings.title: EMPIRICAL CRUX, part 1 — skew is real and large WITHIN a request, but flattens across requests
findings.detail: MoE-Infinity: Leyang Xue, Yao Fu, Zhan Lu, Chuanhao Sun, Luo Mai, Mahesh Marina, 'MoE-Infinity: Efficient MoE Inference on Personal Machines with Sparsity-Aware Expert Cache', arXiv:2401.14361v3, ICML. Measurements: within a single request, in Mixtral's final layer one expert was reused '7 times more than any other expert'; for models with ~100 experts, 'fewer than 5% of experts are repeatedly activated when decoding tokens for a single request'. BUT — and this is the load-bearing negative result — across requests, reuse patterns 'become more uniform', and over 'over 1000 sequences' the authors state 'reuse counts even out over time'. This is precisely why they abandoned model-level tracing in favour of REQUEST-level Expert Activation Matrices (rEAMs): an L x E matrix (L = MoE layers, E = experts/layer) where M[i][j] counts tokens routed to expert E[i,j], accumulated over one prompt+generation. Table 2: k-means over rEAMs finds 10-30 distinct activation GROUPS across BigBench, Flan and MMLU — strong intra-group Euclidean similarity, clear inter-group separation. Critical caveat they state: 'transition probability between groups is low' (max ~0.3), making cross-workload prediction infeasible.
findings.relevance: This is the strongest single piece of evidence AGAINST the naive version of the idea. A global rolling-window hotness histogram — exactly what EPLB collects and what step 1 of the proposal describes — is the model-level statistic MoE-Infinity found flattens toward uniform. If the GG box serves a genuinely mixed workload, the K3->K4 upgrade set may end up near-arbitrary. The idea survives in two regimes: (a) the deployment is workload-HOMOGENEOUS (one user, mostly coding, or mostly VoIP/telephony transcription analysis) so the aggregate never averages out; or (b) the policy operates at rEAM-group granularity rather than globally, which is far harder because group transitions are unpredictable (~0.3) and a bit-width swap cannot be done per-request. Regime (a) is precisely the 'specializes to each user's actual workload' pitch, so the pitch is defensible — but it must be stated as a homogeneity assumption and validated on the user's own 7.3M-token trace before building anything. That validation is cheap and should be the first experiment: bucket the existing collector trace into windows, compute per-expert frequency per window, and measure rank correlation of the top-N set across windows and across days.

findings.title: EMPIRICAL CRUX, part 2 — temporal locality exists but is weak; LFU beats LRU; middle layers are the most skewed
findings.detail: 'In-depth Analysis on Caching and Pre-fetching in Mixture of Experts Offloading', arXiv:2511.05814v1, 8 Nov 2025. Mixtral-8x7B traces: 'distributions are concentrated in a small number of experts rather than evenly distributed', with some experts activated only ONCE across an entire decoding sequence. Figure 7 shows MIDDLE layers are 'more skewed' than early or late layers. Temporal locality: the probability a token picks the same expert as the previous token is above the 12.5% random baseline, 'sometimes near 30%' — but the authors explicitly conclude temporal locality 'does exist, it is not strong' relative to the expert-imbalance effect. Head-to-head cache policies: LRU 29.1% precision / 58.2% recall vs LFU 29.9% / 59.8%; LFU delivered 84.6% faster token generation on an A6000 (2.34 -> 4.32 tok/s). Popular experts are 'selected not always continuously, but still frequently, in intervals', attributed to semantic similarity between tokens within a sequence rather than adjacency.
findings.relevance: Three actionable consequences. (1) FREQUENCY beats RECENCY as the policy signal — which is good news, because a bit-width policy is inherently a frequency policy operating on a slow window; DynaExq's EMA-of-router-probability is the right family. (2) Skew is layer-dependent, so a GLOBAL bit budget across all layers (GEMQ's point) will naturally spend more bits in the middle of the stack; a per-layer uniform budget would waste them. (3) Some experts fire literally once per sequence — those are unambiguous K2 candidates, and the tail is fat enough that downgrading it should fund a meaningful number of K4 upgrades.

findings.title: EMPIRICAL CRUX, part 3 — domain specialization is MODEL-DEPENDENT: Mixtral has none, OLMoE has a lot, and fine-grained/from-scratch is the differentiator
findings.detail: Mixtral of Experts (arXiv:2401.04088): 'no obvious patterns in the assignment of experts based on the topic can be observed'; routing aligns more with SYNTAX than domain; 'the distribution of expert assignment is very similar for all layers for different tasks'. OLMoE (Muennighoff et al., arXiv:2409.02060): the opposite — strong domain specialization with individual experts clearly preferring code vs academic papers vs general text, 'more pronounced than in other MoE models like Mixtral-8x7B, potentially due to training from scratch rather than upcycling'; also strong vocabulary specialization, stronger in later layers. Router saturation: after just 1% of training tokens ~60% of routing decisions are already fixed, later layers saturating faster ('Three Phases of Expert Routing', arXiv:2604.04230, describes surge -> stabilization -> relaxation). DeepSeekMoE (arXiv:2401.06066, ACL 2024) argues fine-grained expert segmentation is what BUYS specialization: splitting each FFN into finer experts lets 'diverse knowledge be decomposed more finely', with shared always-on experts absorbing common knowledge to reduce redundancy among routed experts. Corroborating serving-side measurements: ELDR (arXiv:2607.00466) reports each domain (Code, Math, Medical, Legal) 'over-activates a distinct subset of experts' and that same-domain decode batches activate 21% FEWER distinct experts per step than mixed batches; Director (arXiv:2607.08782) Figure 2 shows expert selection frequency in a single layer 'varies significantly' across request batches from text generation vs math vs code.
findings.relevance: This is the argument that the idea is more likely to work on GLM-5.2 than the Mixtral-era pessimism suggests. GLM-5.2 is 256 routed experts, top-8, DeepSeek-lineage fine-grained-plus-shared — the exact architecture DeepSeekMoE designed to MAXIMIZE per-expert specialization, and the opposite of upcycled Mixtral-8x7B whose 8 coarse experts showed no topical structure. The ELDR 21% figure quantifies the payoff directly: a domain-homogeneous workload touches a materially narrower expert set. Combined with the OLMoE finding that specialization is strongest in LATER layers, this also suggests the upgrade budget should be biased toward late-layer experts. Caveat to state honestly: none of these measure GLM-5.2, and the user's own 7.3M-token layer-78 trace is better evidence than any of them.

findings.title: MoQE — expert layers are far more quantization-robust than dense FFN, validating the asymmetric K3-MoE / K6-dense split
findings.detail: 'Mixture of Quantized Experts (MoQE): Complementary Effect of Low-bit Quantization and Robustness', arXiv:2310.02410 (Microsoft Research). Weight-only quantization applied ONLY to expert weights, down to 2-bit. Core finding: 'expert layers in MoE models are much more robust to the quantization than conventional feedforward networks (FFN) layers' — while attention and dense FFN suffer badly at 2-bit, experts tolerate it. An MoE with 2-bit expert weights outperformed a dense model trained on the same data, at 79.6% size reduction vs FP16, with 1.24x speedup on A100 via an optimized runtime, and 'without any additional training in most cases'.
findings.relevance: Independent validation of the existing GG quantization split (K3 routed experts, BF16/K6 dense+attention) as principled rather than incidental, and it is the reason the fungible-quant budget should be spent almost entirely on routed experts. It also sets expectations for the downgrade direction: K3 -> K2 on cold experts is likely to be survivable precisely because experts are the robust part of the network — which is what makes the budget-freeing side of the proposal viable at all.

findings.title: Matryoshka/nested quantization — the alternative that makes the tensor-size problem disappear, but does not transfer to EXL3 trellis
findings.detail: MatQuant: 'Matryoshka Quantization', arXiv:2502.06786, ICML 2025 (Google DeepMind), also ICLR oral. Insight: integer types are inherently nested — int4 and int2 live in the most significant bits of int8 — so one trained artifact can be SLICED at serve time to any of int8/int4/int2. Extracted int2 models beat standard int2 by up to 4% (OmniQuant base) and 7% (QAT base). Related: MoBiQuant (arXiv:2602.20191), token-adaptive any-precision via a simple threshold adjustment, explicitly 'eliminating the need to store additional scaling factors and extra training overhead'; QuEPT (arXiv:2602.12609), multi-bit switching via cascaded low-rank adapters with one-shot calibration, supporting 'real-time switching between uniform quantization and mixed precision quantization without repeated optimization'; CMPQ (arXiv:2410.13056), channel-wise mixed precision at arbitrary average bit-widths between 2 and 4. A known obstacle across this line: 'precision-dependent outlier migration' — the set of quantization-sensitive tokens changes with precision, hurting cross-bit-width generalization.
findings.relevance: If weights were nested, the whole hard part evaporates: one buffer, fixed byte size, and 'promotion' becomes changing how many bytes the kernel reads — no reallocation, no fragmentation, no atomic swap reserve, no CUDA graph pointer problem, and instant reaction time. This is worth serious thought as an alternative architecture. The blocker is specific and real: EXL3 is a QTIP-derived TRELLIS code with a procedural codebook and Viterbi-searched tail-biting trellises over 16-element vectors in 16x16 tiles — a K3 trellis code is not a prefix of a K4 trellis code, so MSB slicing is meaningless. Making EXL3 nested would be original research (a nested/hierarchical trellis codebook), but it would be a genuinely novel contribution and would dominate the swap-based design on every axis the user is worried about.
