findings.title: vLLM-side mechanics in the local tree: EPLB's fixed-shape assumption is explicit, and the CUDA-graph pointer rule is the real blocker
findings.detail: Confirmed in /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor. (1) /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/distributed/eplb/rebalance_execute.py:550 defines rearrange_expert_weights_inplace; line 598 derives num_local_physical_experts = expert_weights[0][0].shape[0]; lines 608-610 build the exchange buffers as [torch.empty_like(w) for w in first_layer_weights]; and lines 606-607 carry the explicit comment 'NOTE: Currently we assume the same weights across different layers have the same shape.' The whole path is shape-invariant by construction and gated on an ep_group. (2) /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/config/parallel.py:55 EPLBConfig defaults: window_size = 1000, step_interval = 3000 — the exact record-window / decide-interval cadence the proposal describes, already parameterized. (3) /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/distributed/eplb/async_worker.py (188 lines) already implements a background rebalance worker reading global_expert_load_window off the critical path. (4) /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/reload/ (layerwise.py, meta.py, sanitize.py, types.py) is existing in-tree runtime weight-reload machinery using meta-tensor capture/materialize/restore — the closest available hook for replacing weights after startup. (5) vLLM RFC #30359 (QeRL: Online Quantization and Model Reloading) states verbatim: 'As of now, the data pointers used by the cuda graph cannot be updated after capture', so reloaded weights must be COPIED into the existing captured tensors, and regenerating graphs is 'far too slow for the required cadence'. It also notes the existing eager weight-restoration path 'doubles the amount of required memory'.
findings.relevance: Ranks the engineering risks correctly. Fragmentation and swap-reserve are SOLVED problems with a known answer (DynaExq's per-format fixed-block pools). The unsolved one is the CUDA graph: a K3->K4 change alters the tensor's byte size, so it cannot be memcpy'd into a captured buffer, and re-capturing is too slow for a periodic loop. Two escapes, both with precedent: allocate every swappable expert slot at its MAXIMUM bit-width footprint (K4) so the captured pointer and byte size never change and lower bit-widths simply under-fill it — this trades away most of the memory win but makes the mechanism trivial; or keep the MoE expert GEMM outside the captured graph region. Separately, note that EPLB is gated on expert parallelism, which the GG stack explicitly does not use, so none of the existing plumbing is reachable as-is — the load-recording half (window_size/step_interval/expert_load_window) would need to be decoupled from EP first, which is a clean, independently useful upstream contribution.

findings.title: Runtime expert-management systems that are placement/caching only — the field DynaExq departs from
findings.detail: Surveyed via 'A Survey on Inference Optimization Techniques for Mixture of Experts Models' (arXiv:2412.14219). Fiddler: CPU-GPU orchestration, computes experts on CPU rather than moving weights. DAOP (DATE 2025, arXiv:2501.10375): data-aware offloading with predictive pre-calculation, pre-computes experts on CPU one layer ahead; beats Fiddler by 40.4% (4.52 tok/s on Mixtral-8x7B, 8.21 on Phi-3.5-MoE at [256,512]). Pre-gated MoE: restructures the model so layer N's computation identifies layer N+1's experts for preloading. ExpertFlow (arXiv:2510.26730): predictive routing-path-based offloading with adaptive expert scheduling. Klotski: offloading planner using constraint solving and batch scheduling to minimize pipeline bubbles. AdapMoE (ICCAD 2024, DOI 10.1145/3676536.3676741): adaptive sensitivity-based expert gating and management. SiDA-MoE: sparsity-inspired data-aware offloading. Director (arXiv:2607.08782, July 2026): online PROACTIVE expert placement — instead of reacting to historical load like EPLB, it predicts routing for requests already in the queue using either a cascade predictor (77-91% accuracy, <0.1% overhead) or a 4-bit quantized replica of the MoE model as an oracle (91-96% accuracy); explicitly argues reactive systems 'optimize placements based on past patterns' and lag 'rapidly shifting inputs'. CRAFT (arXiv:2603.28768): fine-grained cost-aware expert replication.
findings.relevance: Establishes that expert-granular runtime swapping is a mature, crowded field — the swap plumbing, prefetch predictors and cache policies are all off-the-shelf; only the PRECISION dimension is sparse (DynaExq, HOBBIT/MoE-APEX). Director is the most interesting for the 'trends' half of the proposal: it demonstrates that reactive historical windows lag real workload shifts and that a cheap 4-bit replica of the model can predict routing at 91-96% — which for the GG stack maps neatly onto an asset they already have, the EXL3-quantized MTP layer-78 draft model. Using the already-built 3.7GB draft as the routing oracle for precision scheduling is a concrete, low-cost design that no published system has tried.

findings.title: MoE-I2 and non-uniform per-layer budgets — precedent for search-based allocation of a global compression budget
findings.detail: 'MoE-I2: Compressing Mixture of Experts Models through Inter-Expert Pruning and Intra-Expert Low-Rank Decomposition', arXiv:2411.01016, Findings of EMNLP 2024 (Rutgers et al.). Two stages: inter-expert pruning that first analyzes per-LAYER importance and then applies a NON-UNIFORM pruning ratio per layer, found via Layer-wise Genetic Search plus a Block-wise KT-Reception Field heuristic; then intra-expert low-rank decomposition of surviving experts. Evaluated on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Mixtral-8x7B.
findings.relevance: Not bit-widths, but the closest precedent for the allocation SEARCH the proposal needs when the objective is not linear: when the K2/K3/K4 tradeoff surface is non-convex or the kernel has discrete efficiency cliffs (very likely on SM120 trellis tiles), an LP like MC-MoE's may not be expressible and a genetic/evolutionary search over per-layer budgets is the demonstrated fallback. It also independently confirms that non-uniform per-layer budgets beat uniform ones, reinforcing GEMQ's global-allocation argument.

gaps: TEMPORAL STABILITY OVER LONG HORIZONS IS UNMEASURED ANYWHERE. Every stability measurement I found is within-request (MoE-Infinity rEAMs), within-sequence (arXiv 2511.05814 traces), or within-benchmark. No paper measures whether a given deployment's hot-expert set is stable over hours, days or weeks of real traffic. DynaExq's own paper — the system whose entire premise is long-horizon hotness — provides NO quantitative temporal-stability analysis (no rank correlation across windows, no variance of hotness scores over time) and does not disclose its EMA decay alpha or update period T. This is the single largest evidence gap for the whole idea, and the user's own 7.3M-token layer-78 collector trace is very likely the best dataset in existence to close it.

NO ONLINE RE-QUANTIZATION EXISTS. Every system surveyed (DynaExq, HOBBIT/MoE-APEX, FlexQuant, Mixtral-offloading) stores pre-quantized copies per precision and pages them. I found no system that re-encodes weights from BF16 at runtime. I therefore could not find any data on background re-encode cost, and specifically no measurement of EXL3/QTIP trellis encode throughput (Viterbi search cost per tensor), which determines whether background re-encoding is seconds or minutes per expert. This should be benchmarked locally before committing to the re-encode design over the paged-artifact design.

NOTHING DOES THIS UNDER TENSOR PARALLELISM. DynaExq is explicitly single-GPU (RTX 5090, A6000) and lists distributed integration as future work. HOBBIT/MoE-APEX are edge/single-device (llama.cpp, Jetson). No published system performs runtime precision reallocation under TP, let alone TP4+DCP4 with EP disabled. I found no 'topology-neutral' formulation of a bit-allocation policy anywhere — the closest is AlphaQ's spectral metric, which is topology-independent by accident rather than by design.

NO PROMOTION-LATENCY / REACTION-TIME NUMBERS. DynaExq reports aggregate throughput but never isolates the cost of a precision switch: no time-from-decision-to-availability, no SSD-read + H2D breakdown, no transient buffer size. FlexQuant similarly only claims its PPLE trigger computation is 'negligible'. The user's 'slow reaction time' concern is therefore unquantified in the literature.

THE CLOSED-LOOP FEEDBACK (precision change -> router shift -> hotness change -> precision change) IS UNSTUDIED. The routing-consistency papers (EAQuant, MoEQuant, ExpertQuant, EAC-MoE, GEMQ) all establish that quantization shifts routing, and the runtime papers (DynaExq, HOBBIT) all change precision at runtime, but no paper connects the two. There is zero published analysis of oscillation, hysteresis requirements, or convergence of an online precision-allocation loop.

PER-TENSOR (non-expert) RUNTIME REALLOCATION DOES NOT EXIST IN MoE SYSTEMS. All runtime precision work is expert-granular. The proposal's 'experts/tensors' framing — including dense/attention/MLA tensors and user-pinned tensors — has offline precedent only (EXL3's own per-tensor allocation, CMPQ's channel-wise). FlexQuant is the only runtime layer-granular switcher and it is dense-only, no MoE.

EXL3'S INTERNAL BIT-ALLOCATION OBJECTIVE IS UNVERIFIED. A secondary source (DeepWiki) states EXL3 uses 'layer and tensor level KL-divergence measurements for bit-allocation optimization given a target size' and 'supports arbitrary bitrates by mixing different bit-depths across layers or experts', but the primary doc (exllamav3/doc/exl3.md) explicitly defers: 'A full description of the format is coming, but until then I refer to the code for the quantizer.' I could not confirm the error metric, whether a solver exists, or how MoE experts are specifically handled. Reading exllamav3/conversion/convert_model.py directly is required — this matters because if EXL3 already ships a per-tensor bit-allocation solver, the offline half of the proposal is largely done and only needs a workload-derived importance term.

PARTIAL EXTRACTION ON THREE 2026 PAPERS. GEMQ (2605.23078), AlphaQ (2606.04980) and MODE (2606.17118) were only partially extractable from PDF — I have abstracts and methods but not the numeric result tables, exact bit-width ranges, or per-model breakdowns. AlphaQ's claim that calibration-free beats calibration-based is important enough to the user's premise that it should be verified against its actual tables and released code.

NO CONFIRMED CODE RELEASE FOR DynaExq. EAQuant has public code (github.com/darren-fzq1/EAQuant), MxMoE and AlphaQ reference GitHub repos, and MC-MoE is on OpenReview — but I found no repository for DynaExq, so its dual-pool allocator and stable-handle implementation would have to be reconstructed from the paper's prose.

NO GLM-SPECIFIC OR DSA/MLA-SPECIFIC DATA. All expert-activation measurements are on Mixtral, Qwen3-MoE, DeepSeek-MoE, OLMoE or Qwen1.5-MoE. Nothing measures GLM-5.2's 256-expert top-8 routing, and nothing addresses interaction with MLA/DSA sparse attention or with an MTP speculative-decoding layer — including the question of whether the draft layer's routing statistics are a valid proxy for the target model's (which the user's collector implicitly assumes and which Director's 4-bit-replica-oracle result at 91-96% suggests is plausible but unproven for this pairing).

summary: Runtime weight mutation is well-established in serving engines, but essentially all of it is *value refresh at fixed shape* for RL/RLHF. The single most important finding is local: the vLLM tree at /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor **already ships online re-quantization during serving** — `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:985-998` receives BF16 checkpoint-format weights and runs `initialize_layerwise_reload` / `finalize_layerwise_reload`, which deletes the `_already_called_process_weights_after_loading` guard and re-runs `quant_method.process_weights_after_loading` per layer. So "re-quantize a live model" is a solved, shipped problem; what is *not* solved is changing the resulting tensor's size. Three independent hard walls enforce fixed size: `default_weight_loader` asserts `param.size() == loaded_weight.size()` (weight_utils.py:1182), layerwise reload copies results back into the original storage explicitly "to preserve cudagraph refs" (layerwise.py:240-246), and its own docstring Limitation 4 states the design assumes loaded-weight count equals init-time count. The same constraint appears in EPLB (`rearrange_expert_weights_inplace`) and in TensorRT, whose `Refitter.setNamedWeights` fails on "a change in the weights count". The proposed idea has already been published as **DynaExq (arXiv:2511.15015, Nov 2025)** — runtime EMA-hotness-driven expert precision promotion/demotion under an HBM budget — which solves the resize problem with **partitioned fixed-block dual pools** plus versioned "stable expert handles", not in-place copy. Critically for EXL3 specifically, the MatQuant/Any-Precision "nested bit-width" escape hatch does **not** apply: EXL3 `pack_trellis` produces `256*K//16` words from an independent per-K LDLQ trellis search, so a K3 code is not a prefix of a K4 code.

findings.title: vLLM ALREADY re-quantizes weights during live serving — the layerwise reload path
findings.detail: /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:985-998 branches on `typed_update_info.is_checkpoint_format` and wraps the weight receive in `initialize_layerwise_reload(model)` ... `finalize_layerwise_reload(model, self.model_config)`. The implementation at /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/reload/layerwise.py:206-251 (`_layerwise_process`) materializes the layer from meta, explicitly deletes the re-entry guard (`if hasattr(layer, "_already_called_process_weights_after_loading"): delattr(...)`, lines 221-222), replays cached weight loads, then calls `quant_method.process_weights_after_loading(layer)` (line 238). The public API is `support_quantized_model_reload_from_hp_weights` (reload/torchao_decorator.py:29), documented as: "reloading high precision (bfloat16/float16/float32) weight for an already quantized model, this involves restoring the weights to a high precision weights and then online quantize the weights." Also mirrored at vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:4732-4734.
findings.relevance: This is the exact hook the fungible-quant scheme needs, and it already exists in their tree. Steps 1 (keep BF16 on disk/stream) and 3 (re-encode) map onto an existing, upstream-supported, per-layer code path — they do NOT need to invent live requantization. What they must extend is the size assumption, not the mechanism. It also means the EXL3 quant method would need a `process_weights_after_loading` that is re-entrant and can target a caller-specified K.

findings.title: Three independent hard walls enforce fixed tensor size on every runtime weight path in vLLM
findings.detail: (1) /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_utils.py:1182 — `assert param.size() == loaded_weight.size(), f"Attempted to load weight ({loaded_weight.size()}) into parameter ({param.size()})"`; same assert at vllm/model_executor/layers/linear.py:378. (2) layerwise.py:240-246 comment: "Copy processed values into original tensor storage (preserves cudagraph refs)" followed by `param.data.copy_(getattr(layer, name))` — the storage pointer must survive because CUDA graphs captured raw addresses. (3) reload/__init__.py:14-18 Limitation 4: "This design assumes that the number of weights loaded from disk is the same as the number of weights created at model init time. This is not true for quant methods which (1) pad weights or (2) load qkv weights into the same parameter... future quantizations may cause reloading to fail."
findings.relevance: Confirms and localizes the user's stated asymmetry vs EPLB, at file:line. Wall (2) is the underrated one: even if you solve allocation, a K3→K4 swap re-points the weight tensor, which invalidates captured CUDA graphs. Any design must either keep the pointer stable (fixed-size slot / CUDA VMM remap) or force graph re-capture on swap — and re-capture cost is a per-swap tax the EPLB analogy does not have.

findings.title: DynaExq (arXiv:2511.15015) is the proposed idea, already published — including the memory-resize solution
findings.detail: "Dynamic Expert Quantization for Scalable Mixture-of-Experts Inference" (submitted 19 Nov 2025). Treats single-GPU MoE inference as "an online, budget-constrained precision allocation problem." Hotness metric is an EMA per expert, S_i^(t) = α·S_i^(t-1) + (1-α)·g_i(x_t), capturing "both activation frequency and magnitude, while smoothing short-term spikes"; experts above threshold τ_h (derived from available HBM at init) are promoted. Updates run "periodically rather than per batch, preventing thrashing." Resize is handled by **partitioned dual memory pools** — HBM split into separate high- and low-precision pools with fixed-size blocks aligned to the data format, giving "constant-time and fragmentation-free allocation"; occupancy is indexed CPU-side to avoid runtime cudaMalloc and "eliminate allocator-induced jitter"; a small transient buffer absorbs concurrent promotions. Atomicity is by versioning, not locking: "DynaExq always uses the last stable version of each expert" and if a promotion is in flight "the previous representation remains active." Formats FP16/INT4/INT2 via AutoRound; built on PyTorch + HuggingFace Transformers. Results: Qwen3-80B accuracy 73.09%→77.57%, up to 2.73x throughput vs offload/prefetch baselines at bs=32.
findings.relevance: Direct prior art for steps 1, 2 and 4 of the proposal, and it independently answers all four of the user's stated concerns (swap memory, fragmentation, reaction time, atomicity). The fixed-block dual-pool + versioned-handle design is a ready blueprint. Gaps they can claim: DynaExq is single-GPU HF Transformers (no TP/DCP, no vLLM), uses cheap AutoRound not trellis codes, and its own future-work admits "integration into distributed frameworks" is undone — which is precisely the TP4+DCP4 topology-neutral problem.

findings.title: The MatQuant / Any-Precision nested-bitwidth shortcut does NOT work for EXL3 trellis codes
findings.detail: Matryoshka Quantization (arXiv:2502.06786, PMLR v267 nair25a) exploits that "integer data types, such as int8, inherently possess a nested (Matryoshka) structure where smaller bit-width integers, like int4 or int2, are nested within the most significant bits" — one checkpoint serves 8/4/2-bit by slicing MSBs. Any-Precision LLM (arXiv:2402.10517, ICML 2024 oral, Park et al.) overlays 3,4..n-bit models "into a memory footprint comparable to a single n-bit LLM" with a bitplane-sliced serving engine. But EXL3 is not nested: in exllamav3/modules/quant/exl3_lib/quantize.py, `pack_trellis` computes `packed_shape = (shape[0], shape[1], 256 * K // 16)` and calls a K-specific CUDA packer; each K is a separate LDLQ trellis search over a Hessian-derived LDL decomposition, so K=3 bits are not a prefix of K=4 bits. Per DeepWiki, bitrate is further baked into the codebook ID (e.g. 0xCBAC1FED) and weights use a permuted layout for direct mma.m16n8k16 register loads.
findings.relevance: This is the decisive negative result for the cheapest possible design. If EXL3 were nested, 'fungible quant' collapses to allocating at K_max and masking — no resize, no CUDA-graph invalidation, no background re-encode. It is not. So the user must either (a) accept full re-encode + pool swap (DynaExq-style), or (b) consider a nested-code format (MatQuant-like) as an alternative to EXL3 for the swappable subset only, keeping EXL3 for pinned tensors. Option (b) is a genuinely novel and defensible research direction.

findings.title: Two competing memory patterns from LoRA serving: vLLM's worst-case fixed slots vs S-LoRA's unified paging
findings.detail: vLLM uses worst-case-sized fixed slots. /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/lora/layers/base_linear.py:65-86 allocates `lora_a_stacked = torch.zeros(max_loras, 1, lora_a_out_size, self.input_size, ...)` sized at `lora_config.max_lora_rank`, and `set_lora` (lines 115-120) writes a smaller adapter into a prefix sub-slice: `self.lora_a_stacked[0][index, 0, :lora_a.shape[0], :lora_a.shape[1]].copy_(lora_a, non_blocking=True)`, after `reset_lora(index)` zeroes the slot. By contrast S-LoRA (MLSys 2024, arXiv:2311.03285) introduces "Unified Paging": a single paged pool holding both variable-rank adapter weights and variable-length KV cache, with custom CUDA kernels that "operate directly on non-contiguous memory," explicitly to reduce fragmentation. dLoRA (OSDI '24, Wu et al., usenix.org/conference/osdi24/presentation/wu-bingyang) adds runtime merge/unmerge of adapters into the base model via a credit-based batching algorithm.
findings.relevance: These are the two concrete answers to 'how do I hold a tensor whose size changes'. vLLM's pattern (pre-allocate at K_max, write K3 into a prefix) is trivial to implement and keeps the pointer stable — solving the CUDA-graph problem — but you permanently pay K4 memory, which negates most of the benefit unless K_max is capped tightly. S-LoRA's paging recovers the memory but requires kernels that read non-contiguous pages, and EXL3's mma-permuted register layout makes that hard. dLoRA is the precedent for the *decision policy* being a runtime scheduling problem, not a static config.

findings.title: Every other production engine's runtime weight API is value-refresh only, and TensorRT fails explicitly on size change
findings.detail: TensorRT requires BuilderFlag::kREFIT at build time; then `refitter->setNamedWeights(...)` — and per NVIDIA docs, "setNamedWeights returns false if something goes wrong, such as a wrong weights name or a change in the weights count" (docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/inference-library/refitting-engines.html). vLLM's own RFC #5723 "Add runtime weight update API" proposes only `update_weight(name, dtype, shape)` for RLHF value sync; RFC #31848 standardizes it. SGLang exposes `update_weights_from_tensor(named_tensors, load_format, flush_cache)` and `update_weights_from_distributed` (docs.sglang.io/docs/advanced_features/sglang_for_rl), used for RL rollout sync; LMSYS's P2P update blog (2026-04-29) scales this to 1T params. Notably the transport layer is format-agnostic: /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/distributed/weight_transfer/packed_tensor.py packs to a flat `torch.uint8` stream and unpacks purely from caller-supplied `(name, (shape, dtype))` metadata (lines 112-140) — it never consults the destination parameter.
findings.relevance: Answers 'does anyone change quantization FORMAT at runtime?' — no, nobody in production does. But the packed_tensor finding is encouraging: vLLM's wire protocol can already carry an arbitrarily-sized payload described by caller metadata, so the transport needs zero changes. All the work is in the destination (allocation + loader assert + graph refs). That sharply scopes the engineering.

findings.title: verl's FP8 RL is the closest shipped instance of quantize-on-the-fly at weight-sync time
findings.detail: verl (verl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/low_precision/fp8.html) runs "FP8 rollout-only mode: keeps training in BF16 and quantizes rollout inference to FP8." It does this by monkey-patching vLLM: "we replace the `vllm.model_executor.layers.quantization.fp8.Fp8LinearMethod.process_weights_after_loading` function to handle weight processing after quantization," and notes "For SGLang, this patch is not needed as it natively supports loading quantized weights." The re-entrancy hazard this creates is visible in the local tree: `_already_called_process_weights_after_loading` is set/checked at /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/fp8.py:579, 605, 640, 869, 917, 1099, 1183, 1238 — a guard whose sole purpose is preventing double-quantization on repeated loads.
findings.relevance: Proof that BF16-in / quantized-in-GPU with per-update re-quantization is a real production workload today (every RL step), which de-risks the 'quantize online at startup, re-encode later' half of the plan and gives a performance reference point for how expensive repeated re-quantization is. The guard-flag proliferation is also a warning: their EXL3 quant method will need the same re-entrancy discipline, and getting it wrong silently double-quantizes.

findings.title: Weight streaming and JIT subset delivery are established, but not at chosen-bit-width granularity
findings.detail: TensorRT weight streaming offloads weights to host and streams them to device during execution, enabled via kWEIGHT_STREAMING + kSTRONGLY_TYPED, with `getWeightStreamingAutomaticBudget()` (docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/tensorrt/latest/inference-library/weight-streaming.html); TensorRT-LLM adds weight-stripped/'Weightless' engines refitted from checkpoint at runtime. ZeRO-Inference (deepspeed.ai/2022/09/09/zero-inference.html) pins weights in DRAM/NVMe and "dynamically streams each layer into GPU memory for computation as required." FlexGen (arXiv:2303.06865) solves tensor placement across GPU/CPU/disk via linear programming. For remote JIT: safetensors' 8-byte header-length + JSON header + buffer layout means "it's very simple and efficient to fetch and parse metadata... using small (Range) HTTP requests" (huggingface.co/docs/safetensors/en/metadata_parsing; safetensors issues #44, #443 'Efficient key-wise streaming'). HF Xet uses GearHash content-defined chunking at ~64 KiB with Blake3 MerkleHash and global dedup (huggingface.co/docs/xet/en/chunking, /deduplication).
findings.relevance: Streaming a named subset of tensors from a remote repo by HTTP range read is genuinely established and needs no new infrastructure — the safetensors header gives byte offsets per tensor name. Two caveats for this plan: (1) all the engine-level streaming systems stream a FIXED artifact for capacity reasons, not to change precision, so there is no prior art for 'fetch the K4 version of expert 137 only'; (2) Xet dedup will NOT help here — re-encoding at a different K changes every byte of the trellis, so a K3 and K4 artifact of the same expert share no chunks, meaning a multi-bpw repo costs the full sum of its variants.

findings.title: HOBBIT and FlexQuant: per-expert and per-layer precision swapping already demonstrated
findings.detail: HOBBIT (arXiv:2411.01433, Nov 2024) is "a mixed precision expert offloading system" that works by "dynamically replacing less critical cache-miss experts with low precision versions," across three levels — token-level dynamic expert loading, layer-level adaptive prefetching, sequence-level multidimensional caching. Built on llama.cpp; up to 9.93x decode speedup vs SOTA MoE offloading. FlexQuant (arXiv:2501.07139) generates an ensemble of Elastic Quantization Models sharing parameters between two base quantized models so the ensemble "does not require extra storage cost"; it swaps individual layers between low and high bit-width versions at ~100MB granularity ("15x improvement in transition granularity"), ~13-17GB total policy storage vs 177GB baseline for Llama-2-7B, with a deliberate "one-way design policy" where transitions only go toward lower precision to minimize swap I/O.
findings.relevance: HOBBIT validates that per-expert precision choice at runtime yields large wins, and that the decision can key off cache-miss criticality rather than requiring BF16 activation measurement. FlexQuant's one-way (downgrade-only) policy is a pragmatic simplification worth noting: it avoids the expensive upgrade path entirely. FlexQuant also shows the storage trick of materializing hybrids from two base quants rather than N artifacts — relevant if they keep K3 and K4 repos and mix per-tensor.

findings.title: EXL3 already ships the per-tensor bit-allocation tooling the user calls the 'unsolved hard part'
findings.detail: Per DeepWiki's EXL3 Quantization System page and the exllamav3 repo: "Exllamav3 offers tools to measure per layer (with -l2) or even per-tensor (with -l3) contributions to KL-div improvements," and "the json file can be fed to the optimize.py script with a target bpw to output an optimized quant." EXL3 supports "arbitrary bitrates (e.g., 3.25 bpw) by mixing different bit-depths across layers or experts." The encoding pipeline requires a Hessian: finalize Hessian → LDL decomposition → Hadamard transforms → LDLQ recursion, with `fallback_quant()` (no compensation) used when the Hessian is unavailable.
findings.relevance: Reframes the 'hard part'. A KL-divergence-per-tensor-vs-bpw curve is exactly a marginal-utility table, and a fixed memory budget over marginal utilities is a knapsack — solvable. Two things are genuinely missing rather than unsolved: (a) the KL curve is measured offline against a static calibration set, so it is workload-generic, not workload-specialized (their glm52-mtp78-collector is precisely the machinery to make it workload-specific); (b) the Hessian requirement means online re-encode needs per-expert Hessians accumulated during serving — which is a far cheaper live-collectable statistic than full BF16 activations on rented B300s, and is arguably the strongest novel contribution available here.

findings.title: CUDA VMM in vLLM's sleep mode is the one primitive that could give stable pointers with variable backing
findings.detail: vLLM's CuMemAllocator (/home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/device_allocator/cumem.py) wraps CUDA virtual memory management — `python_create_and_map` / `python_unmap_and_release` (lines 32-33, 59, 62, 214, 293) — and asserts incompatibility with PyTorch's `expandable_segments:True` (line 132). Sleep mode level 1 offloads weights to CPU, level 2 discards them; `wake_up(tags)` (line 228) supports partial wake, e.g. POST /wake_up?tags=weights (docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/sleep_mode/, vllm.ai/blog/2025-10-26-sleep-mode, reporting 18-200x faster than full reload). EPLB's mover, /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/distributed/eplb/rebalance_execute.py:550-576 `rearrange_expert_weights_inplace`, takes tensors "of shape (num_local_physical_experts, hidden_size_i)" and has an `is_profile` flag to "perform dummy communications to reserve enough memory for the buffers."
findings.relevance: cuMemCreate/cuMemMap lets you reserve a virtual address range once and remap different amounts of physical memory under it — the textbook answer to 'tensor changed size but the pointer must not move', and it directly attacks both the CUDA-graph invalidation and the fragmentation concerns. vLLM already links and uses these primitives, so the dependency exists. Nobody has applied them at per-expert granularity for precision changes; that is an open and credible engineering contribution. EPLB's `is_profile` buffer-reservation trick is also the established pattern for pre-reserving the swap scratch the user worried about.

gaps: No published system performs runtime bit-width changes under tensor/context parallelism. DynaExq, HOBBIT, FlexQuant and Any-Precision LLM are all single-GPU. I found nothing on how a precision swap synchronizes across TP4+DCP4 ranks, nor any 'topology-neutral' bit-allocation artifact format. This appears genuinely unexplored and is the user's stated requirement.

No system re-encodes trellis/VQ/codebook-based quantization online. Every runtime-requantization instance found (verl FP8, vLLM layerwise reload, DynaExq/AutoRound, HOBBIT) uses cheap affine or round-to-nearest schemes. I could not find any measurement of the wall-clock cost of an online EXL3/QTIP LDLQ encode for a single expert on SM120, so the feasibility of step 3 (background re-encode) is unquantified.

I could not determine whether vLLM's CUDA graph capture can tolerate a re-pointered weight tensor, or what the re-capture cost would be per swap. The layerwise.py:240 comment proves the current design avoids the question rather than answering it; I found no issue or RFC discussing it.

DynaExq's promotion/demotion window size T is not numerically stated in the paper, and I could not verify whether code is released. My reading came from the arXiv HTML render, not a peer-reviewed version — as of Aug 2026 I found no venue acceptance.

I did not verify llama.cpp's or HF TGI's runtime weight-update surface directly. HOBBIT is built on llama.cpp but that is a research fork; whether upstream llama.cpp or TGI expose any live weight-replacement API is unconfirmed. Similarly I did not confirm whether ExLlamaV3 itself has any hot-swap or multi-bitrate-resident capability.

Whether EXL3 K3 and K4 encodings of the same tensor could be made to share the Hessian/LDL computation (amortizing re-encode cost across bit-widths) is not addressed anywhere I found — I inferred the non-nested property from pack_trellis and the per-K LDLQ sweep, but did not find an authoritative statement from turboderp.

Two arXiv PDFs (2511.15015 and 2501.07139) failed to parse as PDF; I recovered both via arxiv.org/html renders. Direct quotes from those two should be re-verified against the canonical PDFs before being cited in any writeup.

No prior art found for the 'pin certain tensors at high fidelity' user-facing control, nor for persisting and rehydrating a learned bit-allocation across restarts. These parts of the proposal appear to have no analogue in the literature.

summary: No existing vLLM RFC, issue, or PR proposes workload-driven runtime bit-width reallocation of weights — the contribution is NOT a duplicate. The closest work splits cleanly into three non-overlapping halves that all stop short of the idea: (1) online quantization, which is now a mature and actively-developed subsystem (RFC #32029/#32412 closed, RFC #50281 open with PRs #50401/#51285) but is strictly static, decided once at startup from config, and — verified in the local tree — never cached to disk; (2) EPLB (PR #18343), which supplies exactly the periodic-window/rearrange loop the proposal wants to imitate, but whose transport hard-codes fixed shapes via `torch.empty_like` and is already breaking on mere quantization *metadata* dtypes (open bug #51567), confirming the stated K3→K4 size-change asymmetry is real and unaddressed; and (3) the RL weight-reload stack (#31848, #48920, #48312), whose brand-new `WeightLoadSession` abstraction explicitly scopes EPLB rebalance and non-checkpoint shape changes OUT. Two adjacent proposals contain most of the missing runtime machinery but never touch weight precision: #38256 (per-expert LFRU hotness + async H2D + atomic swap, explicitly "quant-agnostic") and #49198 (async re-quantize into lower-precision tier + atomic remap — but for KV cache blocks, not weights). EXL3 specifically has no upstream presence: #19896 was closed as not planned, and #39583 signals maintainers want exotic quant formats moved OUT of tree into plugins.

findings.title: DUPLICATE CHECK VERDICT: no duplicate exists — no RFC/PR in vLLM proposes runtime bit-width reallocation driven by observed workload
findings.detail: Exhaustive GitHub search across vllm-project/vllm issues and PRs for: requantization/re-quantize (106 PR hits), 'adaptive quantization'/'adaptive precision' (14 issue hits), 'bit width'/'bpw'/'bits per weight' (20 hits), 'per-expert' + precision (116 hits), dynamic+quantization+experts+upgrade/downgrade+memory budget (0 hits), EPLB+quantization+size (6 hits, all bugs). Zero results describe periodically re-deciding per-tensor bit-widths at runtime under a memory budget. The only issue combining 'dynamic' + 'bit-width' + 'weights' is #30359, which is about memory-efficient reloading, not bit-width change.
findings.relevance: Satisfies AGENTS.md section 1 'Duplicate-work checks'. The fungible-quant RFC can be filed as genuinely novel. The two AGENTS.md gh commands to run before filing are `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "online quantization"` and `--search "EPLB rearrange"`; both return the neighbors listed below, none of which claim this scope.

findings.title: CLOSEST NEIGHBOR (open, active): RFC #50281 'Per-layer online quantization configuration' + PRs #50401, #51285 — static per-layer scheme selection, no runtime change, no per-expert, no disk cache
findings.detail: Author fxmarty-amd, 2026-07-29, OPEN. Proposes `--quantization-config.online '{"re:.*self_attn.*":"fp8","re:.*kv_b_proj.*":"mxfp4"}'` — regex/exact layer-name patterns mapping to online quant schemes, with conflict detection and precedence over legacy `--quantization`. Implementation PR #50401 (2026-07-30, open); a competing/overlapping PR #51285 '[Online quantization] Add targeted online quantization configuration based on user patterns' (2026-08-06, open); plus #51392 'Support online quantization with partially pre-quantized checkpoints' (2026-08-07, open). Explicitly does NOT cover per-expert bit-width, runtime/dynamic changes, or disk caching.
findings.relevance: This is the single most important PR to cite in the fungible-quant RFC's 'why this is not duplicating an existing PR' section. It is the natural *substrate*: it establishes the per-layer-pattern → scheme mapping vocabulary. The fungible-quant proposal is the dynamic, statistics-driven, per-expert extension of exactly this static map. Framing it as 'make #50281's mapping mutable at runtime and let vLLM author it from observed load' is the cleanest positioning and avoids stepping on fxmarty-amd's work. Note two PRs already race on this surface — coordinate rather than add a third.

findings.title: Online quantization at startup EXISTS and is mature, but results are NEVER cached to disk — verified in local tree
findings.detail: vLLM supports `--quantization fp8` (and mxfp4, nvfp4, fp8_ptpc, block_fp8, mxfp8, TurboQuant) over a BF16 checkpoint via `process_weights_after_loading`, plus a newer memory-lean path that quantizes inside the `weight_loader` hook as tensors stream in. ~57 PRs in the 'online quantization' title search. Verified locally: `grep -rln "quant.*cache_dir|cache.*quantized_weights|save_quantized" vllm/` returns NOTHING; `docs/features/quantization/fp8.md` only documents `model.save_pretrained(SAVE_DIR)` as an *offline llm-compressor* step, not an engine-side cache. Every restart re-quantizes from scratch. Known pain: #48035 reports official FP8 checkpoints are ~40% slower at bs=1 than runtime-quantized ones; #46611 users hit 60s shared-memory broadcast timeouts blamed on 'compilation, weight/kv cache quantization'.
findings.relevance: Directly confirms the proposal's 'quantize online at startup, cache the result locally' half is (a) half-built already — the quantize step exists — and (b) genuinely missing its other half. A standalone 'cache online-quantized weights to VLLM_CACHE_ROOT' PR is small, uncontroversial, immediately useful to everyone (not just EXL3 users), and is the ideal first landable increment that de-risks the larger RFC.

findings.title: The disk-cache pattern to imitate: torch_compile_cache under VLLM_CACHE_ROOT, keyed by a config `compute_hash()` factor digest
findings.detail: vLLM already ships exactly the cache architecture a quant cache needs. `vllm/compilation/backends.py:962` builds `os.path.join(envs.VLLM_CACHE_ROOT, "torch_compile_cache", hash_key)`; `vllm/compilation/decorators.py:460` documents `VLLM_CACHE_ROOT/torch_compile_cache/torch_aot_compile/{hash}`; the key comes from `CompilationConfig.compute_hash()` (`vllm/config/compilation.py:697-727`) which calls `get_hash_factors(self, ignored_factors)` then `hash_factors(...)`, explicitly folding in nested `pass_config.compute_hash()` and `dynamic_shapes_config.compute_hash()`, and explicitly *ignoring* selected fields. `VLLM_CACHE_ROOT` defaults to `~/.cache/vllm` (`vllm/envs.py:33`, `:545`). Sibling caches already exist: `VLLM_XLA_CACHE_PATH` (`envs.py:55`), `VLLM_ASSETS_CACHE` (`envs.py:62`). `compiler_interface.py:650` even shows the user-facing recovery advice pattern ('remove ~/.cache/vllm/torch_compile_cache and try again').
findings.relevance: This is the strongest 'we already do this' argument available and it is precisely the topology-neutrality lever. The compile cache's `ignored_factors` mechanism is the existing, blessed way to say 'this factor must NOT enter the key'. A quant cache should deliberately EXCLUDE tp_size/dcp_size/device_count from its hash so a cached quant survives a TP4→TP2 change — mirroring how the compile cache already discriminates which config fields matter. Cite these exact line numbers in the RFC; reviewers respond well to 'imitate the existing cache' over 'invent a new one'.

findings.title: EPLB origin: PR #18343 by abmfy, merged 2025-06-26 — supplies the exact periodic window/interval loop the proposal wants, with NO stated intent to generalize beyond expert placement
findings.detail: '[Feature] Expert Parallelism Load Balancer (EPLB)', author abmfy (Bowen Wang), merged 2025-06-26 by WoosukKwon, porting DeepSeek's EPLB for auxiliary-loss-free V3/R1 routing. Config surface documented at docs/serving/expert_parallel_deployment.md:135-187: `window_size` (default 1000 engine steps of load history), `step_interval` (default 3000 steps between rebalances), `num_redundant_experts`, `use_async`, `policy`. Local code confirms the loop: `vllm/distributed/eplb/eplb_state.py` holds `expert_load_window_size` (:270), `expert_rearrangement_step` (:275) 'Will trigger a rearrangement if it exceeds the threshold' (:278), `expert_rearrangement_step_interval` (:285), a `rearrange_event` threading.Event for the async worker (:294), initial progress seeded at 3/4 of interval (:464-469), and the trigger at :633 `if self.expert_rearrangement_step >= self.expert_rearrangement_step_interval: ... self.rearrange()`. Generalization: the PR's stated generality is only the per-model `MixtureOfExperts` protocol (expose configs + weight access without model-specific hardcoding) — NOT a reusable periodic-adaptation framework. Follow-on RFC #32028 'EPLB Implementation Refactoring' (ilmarkov, 2026-01-09, open, stale) explicitly does NOT propose generalizing the machinery for other subsystems; it is internal cleanup (fork-join threads, an `AsyncTransferState` enum, terminology 'physical experts'→'expert slots').
findings.relevance: Confirms the analogy is architecturally sound AND that nobody has claimed the generalization. The RFC should propose factoring out the observe-window → decide → apply-async loop as shared infrastructure, citing #32028's refactor as the moment to do it (coordinate with ilmarkov). Also note the docs already warn EPLB 'may not be a good fit for memory constrained environments' (expert_parallel_deployment.md:184) — the same objection will be raised against a swap buffer, so pre-empt it with the fixed-budget framing.

findings.title: CONFIRMED in code: EPLB's transport hard-codes identical shapes (`torch.empty_like`) — and open bug #51567 shows it already fails on quantization metadata alone
findings.detail: `vllm/distributed/eplb/rebalance_execute.py:604-610` allocates the exchange buffers as `weights_buffer = [torch.empty_like(w) for w in first_layer_weights]` under the comment 'NOTE: Currently we assume the same weights across different layers have the same shape.' Reinforced by asserts at :529-533 and :592-602 (`old_layer_indices.shape == new_layer_indices.shape`, `num_physical_experts == ep_size * num_local_physical_experts`). Independently, open bug #51567 'EPLB fails to transport E8M0 expert state' (liuyao0322, 2026-08-09) reports engine init crashing with 'Input tensor data type is not supported for NCCL process group: Float8_e8m0fnu' when MXFP4 Marlin converts weight scales to E8M0; the diagnosis is that 'EPLB currently passes each tensor's numerical dtype directly to its transport. However, EPLB only needs to copy expert state bit-for-bit', with the proposed fix being a storage-preserving `tensor.view(torch.uint8)`.
findings.relevance: This is the load-bearing evidence for the RFC's central 'critical technical asymmetry' claim, and it is stronger than expected: EPLB cannot currently move a same-shape quantized expert, let alone a different-sized one. Cite #51567 as proof the fixed-shape/opaque-bytes gap is already causing user-visible breakage — that reframes the proposal from 'speculative feature' to 'the general fix for a class of bugs vLLM is hitting today'. The uint8-view idea in #51567 is also the right primitive for K3/K4 payloads: treat expert state as opaque byte blobs with a length, not typed tensors.

findings.title: NEAREST RUNTIME-MACHINERY PRECEDENT: RFC #38256 'Incremental MoE Expert Offloading — GPU Cache + Async Pipeline' has per-expert hotness + async swap + atomic replace, but is explicitly quant-agnostic
findings.detail: Author e1n00r, 2026-03-26, OPEN, with PR #37190 in review (~980 LOC, CI passing) and PRs 2-3 planned. Expert weights live in CPU pinned memory; a fixed-size GPU cache holds hot experts. Eviction is LFRU with explicit runtime scoring: `score = freq / age`, 'Lower score = evict first', designed to preserve high-traffic 'hub' experts across workload shifts. PR 1 is synchronous H2D; PR 2 adds 'Async H2D via CUDA stream + cross-layer temporal prediction'; PR 3 adds a disk tier, more quants, telemetry. Crucially: the design is 'Quant-agnostic' — the cache stores tensors as opaque blobs keyed by name and preserves original precision. Companion request #41447 '--moe-gpu-prefetch <num>' (leoustc, 2026-05-01, open/stale) proposes slot_to_expert / expert_to_slot maps with LRU-or-frequency victim selection, also with no precision dimension.
findings.relevance: This is the proposal's closest structural sibling and its best potential ally rather than a competitor: it independently builds per-expert runtime hotness statistics, an async background transfer pipeline, and an atomic swap of expert weights during serving — i.e. three of the four hard pieces the fungible-quant idea needs. The fungible-quant RFC adds the one axis #38256 deliberately omits: precision. Strongly consider proposing the two compose (its 'opaque blob keyed by name' cache is already the right shape for variable-size K3/K4 payloads) and CC e1n00r. This also weakens the 'vLLM loads weights once at startup' objection — #37190 already breaks that assumption in review.

findings.title: STRONGEST CONCEPTUAL PRECEDENT: #49198 proposes exactly the async-requantize-then-atomically-remap lifecycle — for KV cache blocks instead of weights
findings.detail: '[Feature]: Recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache', XAEAZii, 2026-07-20, OPEN. Blocks live in tiered precision pools and move unidirectionally tier[0]→tier[1]→...→tier[n-1]. Lifecycle: allocate/write new blocks in the highest tier; when a completed block 'crosses a configured age boundary, it could be asynchronously quantized and moved to the next lower-precision pool'; allocate a page in the next tier, 'Quantize/copy the block asynchronously', atomically update the logical→physical mapping, then release the source page. No maintainer responses yet. Companion adaptive-precision KV proposals: #38930 'Entropy-adaptive per-head KV cache quantization: +8% quality over uniform at same compression' (open), #39416 phase-aware KV quant for reasoning models (closed), #46613 / #44578 KVarN 4-bit K / 2-bit V (open).
findings.relevance: Near-perfect architectural template — same four steps the fungible-quant idea needs (observe → async re-encode at a new bit-width → atomic pointer swap → free the old buffer), differing only in what is being re-encoded. Cite it to show the *mechanism* is already considered reasonable in vLLM and to borrow its indirection trick: the atomic swap works because there is a logical→physical mapping layer, so the size change is absorbed by the allocator rather than by an in-place copy. That is the direct answer to the EPLB `empty_like` asymmetry — weights need the same logical→physical indirection EPLB lacks and #49198 assumes. Caveat: #49198 has no maintainer buy-in yet, so it is precedent for the design, not for acceptance.

findings.title: The RL weight-reload stack (#31848, #48920, #48312, #30359) is the runtime weight-replacement plumbing — but #48920 explicitly scopes EPLB rebalance and non-checkpoint shape changes OUT
findings.detail: RFC #31848 'Native Weight Syncing APIs' (hao-aaron, SumanthRH, 2026-01-07, OPEN): POST /init_weight_transfer (NCCL or IPC process groups), POST /update_weights (accepts `dtype_names` and `shapes`, loads incrementally to avoid OOM), POST /finalize_weight_update (runs post-processing for quantization/kernel formats). Impl PRs #31943 (NCCL), #34171 (IPC), #40828 (K8s shared memory, ~20 GB/s). RFC #48920 'Unify the Weight Loading Lifecycle Across Initial Load and Reload' (aoshen02, 2026-07-17, OPEN, draft PR #48908) introduces a `WeightLoadSession` with a 'prepare -> source-specific load or transfer -> finish' boundary, one active session per model, format-based opt-in, structural abort on failure — but states the limitation directly: 'LoRA add/remove, EPLB expert rebalance, sleep/wake, and KV-cache operations do not replace the base checkpoint', and re-quantization runs at finalization 'only within the existing model geometry'. Surrounding: #48312 'Weight Reload Correctness for RL', #48478 'Fail-Closed Graph Storage Contract for Weight Reload', #49090 'Move MTP completeness validation to the weight-update transaction boundary', #48314 '[Roadmap] 2026 Q3 vLLM x RL'. QeRL RFC #30359 (kylesayrs, 2025-12-09, CLOSED, PR #32133) added `layerwise_restore_and_process` to cut peak memory on quantized reload — no bit-width change, no disk cache; note PR #38446 reverted '[QeRL] Compose online quantization with quantized reloading' (#38032), so this area is churny.
findings.relevance: Two-edged and important to handle explicitly in the RFC. Positive: /update_weights already carries per-tensor `dtype_names` + `shapes`, so an API for pushing differently-shaped tensors into a live model partially exists, and #31848's init/update/finalize transaction is the right atomicity model to reuse for hot-swap. Negative: #48920's exclusion list is the exact boundary the proposal must cross, so a reviewer will point at it. Best move is to propose fungible-quant as a *fourth* WeightLoadSession source rather than a bypass, and to engage aoshen02 during #48920's open feedback period before it hardens the 'existing model geometry' assumption into merged code.

findings.title: Sleep mode / CuMemAllocator: the virtual-memory primitive that answers the fragmentation and swap-buffer objections
findings.detail: Origin PR #11743 '[Core] Support fully transparent sleep mode' (youkaichao, 2025-01-05, merged), built on CuMemAllocator using cuMemMap/cuMemUnmap so physical pages can be released while virtual addresses stay valid; #12987 added the /sleep and /wake_up endpoints and V1 support; #12695 ported to ROCm; #14678 added a level-3 sleep that offloads tensors to disk. Tag-based partial wake exists (`wake_up(tags=["weights"])`, see #44395). RFC #15254 'Better support for weight updating while waking up from sleep mode for RLHF' is the sleep↔weight-update crossover. Newer: RFC #34303 'CUDA Checkpoint/Restore for Near-Zero Cold Starts' (2026-02-11, open) with merged PR #44074 '[Core] Pluggable sleep-mode backend abstraction (RFC #34303)' and CLI plumbing #45506; PR #40897 'Sleep 3 — Keep weights on GPU, discard KV cache'; #33930 'GPU Memory Snapshotting to reduce cold starts'. Directly relevant to the user's hardware: #21336 'vLLM crashes when using --enable-sleep-mode with Blackwell PRO 6000 GPUs' (OPEN since 2025-07-21) and #48680 (sleep mode OOMs an NVFP4 model on SM120 due to cumem MemPool overhead).
findings.relevance: CuMemAllocator's map/unmap is the correct mechanism for a variable-size weight swap: reserve a virtual range per expert sized for the max bit-width, and map/unmap physical pages as K3↔K4 changes the payload. That directly answers the user's own 'memory reserved for atomic swap' and 'fragmentation' concerns without a full duplicate buffer, and PR #44074's pluggable sleep-backend abstraction is the seam to hook into. Serious caveat for this user specifically: #21336 says sleep mode is broken on their exact GPU (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) and is still open, so any CuMemAllocator-based design must be validated on SM120 before being promised.

findings.title: EXL3/exllamav3 has ZERO upstream presence, and #39583 shows maintainers are pushing exotic quant formats OUT of tree
findings.detail: #19896 '[Feature]: EXL3 support' (Teeeto, 2025-06-20) — CLOSED as not planned, went stale with no PR and no maintainer engagement. Predecessors all closed with no implementation: #3203 'ExLlamaV2: exl2 support', #296 'Feature request: support ExLlama', #2645 'Question: Would a PR integrating ExLlamaV2 kernels with AWQ be accepted?', #11416 '[Feature]: QTIP Quantization' (QTIP being the trellis scheme EXL3 derives from). PR search for exl3/exllama/trellis/QTIP returns no implementation PR, open or closed. Direction of travel: #39583 '[RFC]: Migrate bitsandbytes and GGUF quantization support to OOT plugin' (open) and #30136 '[RFC]: Deprecate Legacy Quantization Formats' (closed) both push non-core formats out of tree; #50646 is a docs PR on 'entry-point registration and checkpoint-driven selection for OOT quantization'. Nearest in-tree cousin: draft PR #50168 'LUT-B quantization accuracy prototype' (mgoin — a core maintainer — 2026-07-28), implementing NVIDIA Rubin LUT-B as 512 3-bit indices + an 8-entry E4M3 codebook per 8x64 tile (~3.125 bpw, up to 3.516 with residual_8; GSM8K 75.51% vs 52.08% for naive online BF16→LUT-B). It does not reference QTIP/EXL3/trellis.
findings.relevance: Two consequences. First, do NOT bundle EXL3 support into the fungible-quant RFC — upstream has declined EXL3 four times and is actively de-scoping such formats; the RFC must be format-agnostic (defined over 'a quant backend that can re-encode tensor T at bit-width b') with EXL3 as an out-of-tree plugin, or it inherits a settled rejection. Second, #50168 is a significant opening: a core maintainer is prototyping a codebook/LUT scheme at 3.1-3.5 bpw — the same bpw band and the same per-tile-codebook shape as EXL3 K3. Its calibration-free accuracy gap (52% → 75.5% depending on variant) is precisely the 'which tensors deserve the bits' problem the user identifies as unsolved, so mgoin is the natural reviewer and #50168 is the strongest hook for making the bit-allocation argument in language upstream already cares about.

findings.title: Mixed bit-widths WITHIN one MoE layer are demonstrably fragile today — pre-existing bugs the RFC must acknowledge
findings.detail: #41955 '[Bug]: Mixed INT4/INT8 GPTQ MoE models crash on initialization (AssertionError in fused_marlin_moe)' (open) — the fused MoE kernels assume one uniform bit-width across all experts in a layer. #46311 'INCConfig doesn't support hybrid INT4+FP8 AutoRound checkpoints' (open). #49893 'SpeculativeConfig method="draft_model" cannot load mixed-precision compressed-tensors checkpoints (config_groups)' (open). #49552 'MTP draft model ignores checkpoint per-layer quantization config' with fix PR #49553 for Qwen3.5 MTP. #51197 notes a BF16 GDN backbone left unquantized accounts for ~80% of per-step reads.
findings.relevance: This is the most likely technical objection and it lands before any of the swap machinery matters: even a STATIC mixed K3/K4 expert layout would crash the current fused MoE kernels, which assume uniform bit-width per layer. The RFC needs a credible answer — e.g. bucket experts by bit-width and issue one grouped GEMM per bucket, or require the backend to declare mixed-width support. The MTP-specific bugs (#49552/#49893) are also directly relevant to the user's GLM-5.2 layer-78 MTP quant work and are worth filing against or subscribing to independently.

findings.title: Adjacent EPLB-family RFCs worth CC-ing, none overlapping: #49702 (platform backend), #42515 (elastic EP), #44996 (fast EP resize), #30696 (per-instance metrics)
findings.detail: #49702 'Add an EPLB Platform Backend for out-of-tree accelerators' (freyfwt, 2026-07-24, OPEN, feedback through 2026-08-18): adds `Platform.get_eplb_backend_cls()` returning an `EplbPlatformBackend` that owns logical→physical mapping, the load-recording callable, stream/event primitives, and 'allocation and movement operations for weight tensors'; notably it 'Accepts either aggregated tensors or sequences of per-expert tensors, preserving persistent storage structures', while upstream retains control of load windows, placement policy, and transfer plans. #42515 'External Elastic EP Scaling' (lqh-hh, 2026-05-13, open): externally-launched ranks join an EEP transition, transfer expert state, resync KV capacity, switch comm groups and run an EPLB reshuffle — runtime topology change without restart, but reuses existing EEP ops rather than generalizing. #44996 'Fast Runtime Resize of a Pre-Built EP Topology' (open). #30696 'Per-instance EPLB metrics' (open). #31671 topology-aware placement from omni-infer (open). Note the user's stack runs TP4+DCP4 with EP disabled, so all EP-gated paths are inapplicable as-is.
findings.relevance: #49702 is the single best integration seam found: it is the only open proposal that abstracts 'allocation and movement operations for weight tensors' behind a replaceable backend interface, and it already contemplates per-expert tensor sequences rather than one aggregated tensor. If that interface lands describing sizes rather than assuming `empty_like`, variable-bit-width swap becomes implementable without forking EPLB. Its feedback window closes 2026-08-18 — eight days out — so commenting there is the highest-leverage, lowest-cost action available right now, ahead of writing the full RFC. Separately: because the user runs EP=1, the fungible-quant RFC should be careful to define its statistics and swap path independent of expert parallelism, or it will be unusable on their own hardware.
