summary: EXL3 is a QTIP-derived tail-biting trellis code operating on 16x16 weight tiles (256 weights) after 128-point blockwise Hadamard rotations on both sides. Encoding is an exhaustive Viterbi search over a 2^(16-K)-state trellis whose per-tile cost is EXACTLY CONSTANT in K (2^16 branch metrics per step x 256 steps x 2 tail-biting passes ~= 131k branch evaluations per weight, whatever K is) — so a K3->K4 upgrade costs the same GPU time as a K4->K3 downgrade, roughly 1.5-2 s per GLM-sized expert tensor at the ~5M weights/s observed in real conversion logs. The decisive answer to the prefix question is NO, emphatically: each weight's decoded value is a 16-bit sliding window over the bitstream, and only the STRIDE changes with K (3 vs 4 bits per symbol). Truncating a K4 stream to 3 bits per symbol yields entirely different 16-bit windows, and the codebook is a multiply-and-bit-twiddle hash (`x *= 0xCBAC1FED`) with zero locality, so truncation produces uncorrelated noise, not a coarser approximation. Every K change requires a full re-encode from the original BF16 weight PLUS the layer's Hessian, plus fresh `suh`/`svh` metadata (the global scale is found by test-quantizing at the target K). Bit allocation IS natively per-tensor and integer-only (K in 1..8), recorded per-module in `quantization_config.json`, and exllamav3 ships a measure/optimize/compile pipeline that builds mixed-bitrate checkpoints purely by SELECTING tensors from several pre-quantized model directories — no re-encode at all — which is by far the cheapest implementation path for the fungible-quant idea. The hard blocker for per-expert mixing upstream is `multilinear.py:26`, which hard-asserts uniform K across an entire expert bank; the GG fork already routes around this with a two-tier b12x `mixed_trellis` megakernel driven by a `bits_per_expert` JSON map.

findings.title: The algorithm: 16x16 tiles, tail-biting Viterbi over a 2^(16-K)-state trellis, 128-point Hadamards
findings.detail: `quantize_tiles_kernel.cuh` is the encoder core. Per 16x16 tile (256 weights, permuted into tensor-core lane order by `tensor_core_perm`): `constexpr int Kr = 16 - K; constexpr int max_q = 1 << K; constexpr int edges = 65536 >> K;`. The 16-bit register S_t is the codeword window; the transition is `state0 = (k << Kr) | out_edge_idx` with `in_edge_idx = state0 >> K`, i.e. S_t = ((S_{t-1} << K) | K_new_bits) mod 2^16. The value is `decode_3inst<cb>(encoded)` where `encoded = (prev_edge << K) | edge` reconstructs the full 16-bit window. Tail-biting is enforced by running `forward(128, -1); end_state = backward(128, false, argmin_cost()); forward(0, end_state); backward(0, true, end_state)` — two full forward passes. Hadamards: `had_k, had_n = 128, 128` (quantize.py:15), applied blockwise left and right in `regularize()` (quantize.py:1205, 1212) along with per-input-channel and per-output-channel RMS scales and random sign flips (su/sv). Codebooks are procedural 3-instruction hashes selected per tensor: cb0 `3inst`, cb1 `mcg` (x *= 0xCBAC1FED), cb2 `mul1` (x *= 0x83DCD12D, default) — see `codebook.cuh:56-90` and `--codebook` default "mul1" (convert_model.py:49).
findings.relevance: Establishes the atomic unit of re-encoding: one 16x16 tile = 256 weights = one self-contained cyclic codeword. Tiles are independently decodable (the `% (bits*256/32)` wrap in exl3_dq.cuh confirms per-tile cyclic addressing), which is why TP slicing of the trellis at 16-column granularity works (exl3.py:303). Any fungible-quant scheme inherits that granularity for free.

findings.title: CRUCIAL: a K3 code is NOT a prefix or subset of a K4 code — truncation destroys the weight
findings.detail: The decode window is ALWAYS 16 bits wide regardless of K; only the stride changes. From `exl3_dq.cuh:16-31`: `int b0 = t_offset * bits + bits - 16 + 256 * bits; ... uint32_t a = ptr[i0 % (bits * 256 / 32)]; ... return decode_3inst<cb>(w0);`. Weight t reads bits [t*K + K - 16, t*K + K) of the tile's 256*K-bit cyclic stream. At K=4 that window spans weight t plus the previous 3 weights; at K=3 it spans weight t plus the previous ~4.33 weights. Reading a K4 stream with stride 3 produces completely different windows. Worse, the codebook is a hash — `x *= 0xCBAC1FEDu; lop3.b32 %0, %0, 0x8fff8fff, 0x3b603b60, 0x6a; __hadd(low, high)` — so a single flipped bit in the window yields an uncorrelated Gaussian sample, not a nearby value. There is no monotone/embedded structure. Additionally the state space differs (8192 states at K3 vs 4096 at K4), the Viterbi-optimal path differs, and `su`/`sv` differ because the global scale `g_scale` is found by test-quantizing sample tiles AT THE TARGET K (`g_scale_gss` -> `g_scale_search_batch` -> `quantize_tiles` with `quant_args["K"]`, quantize.py:1045-1071, 1215-1220) and is then folded into `su` (`su /= g_scale`).
findings.relevance: This kills the cheap-downgrade hypothesis outright. Every K transition — up OR down — is a full re-encode requiring the original BF16 weight AND a Hessian. It also means the BF16 weights (or a second pre-quantized variant) must remain available on disk or be streamed; you cannot derive K3 from a resident K4 tensor.

findings.title: Encoding compute cost is EXACTLY INDEPENDENT of K
findings.detail: Per Viterbi step the kernel evaluates `edges * max_q = 2^(16-K) * 2^K = 65536` branch metrics — constant. Times 256 steps times 2 tail-biting forward passes = 33,554,432 branch metrics per 256-weight tile = 131,072 branch-metric evaluations per weight, for every K from 1 to 8. What DOES change with K is the Viterbi scratch memory: `temp_edges` is `(max_batch, 256, 65536 >> K)` int16 → 4 MiB/tile at K3, 2 MiB at K4, 8 MiB at K2. The source comment is explicit: "At K >= 4 the temp buffers are cheap enough to size for full occupancy on large GPUs (+17% throughput on GB202 at big batches); at lower K, temp_edges is multiple GB already and 256 stays the cap" — so `max_batch_size = max(256, 2 * SM_count)` only for K>=4. On a 188-SM RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell that is 376 tiles in flight (752 MiB) at K4 vs 256 tiles (1 GiB) at K3.
findings.relevance: Direct answer to 'how expensive is a re-encode': upgrading K3->K4 costs the same GPU-seconds as downgrading K4->K3. There is no cheap direction. Also: at K4+ the encoder actually runs ~17% faster on Blackwell because of the occupancy bump, and uses LESS scratch VRAM — mildly favourable for an online upgrade path on the user's hardware.

findings.title: Measured encode throughput: ~5M weights/s per GPU (real conversion logs), ~1.5-2 s per GLM expert tensor
findings.detail: Upstream issue #112 (PrimeIntellect-INTELLECT-3, Glm4MoeForCausalLM, 5.76 bpw decoder / 6 head, cal 250x2048) shows per-tensor times: q_proj [9.13 s] and o_proj [10.49 s] (4096x12288 = 50.3M weights → 4.8-5.5M w/s), dense mlp up_proj [8.23 s] / down_proj [8.69 s] (4096x10944 = 44.8M → 5.2-5.4M w/s), k_proj/v_proj [1.35 s] (4.2M → 3.1M w/s, small tensors underfill the GPU). Full layer 0 = [78.07-80.01 s] for ~243M weights = ~3.1M w/s INCLUDING the Hessian-capture forward pass. Kimi-Dev-72B (issue #52) shows `model.layers.79 [68.06 s]`. README claim: "a couple of minutes for smaller models, up to a few hours for larger ones (70B+) on a single RTX 4090 or equivalent". Extrapolating to a GLM-5.2 routed expert (5120x1536 = 7.86M weights): ~1.5 s per tensor, ~4.7 s for a full expert (gate+up+down) on the single-tensor path. Note the batched MoE path (`quantize_exl3_batch` + `ldlq_batched`) is materially faster because it feeds `quantize_tiles` large batches instead of one small tensor at a time.
findings.relevance: Sets the reaction-time budget. Re-encoding a single expert is seconds, not minutes — genuinely viable as a background task. But re-encoding a meaningful FRACTION of 256 experts x ~90 layers is hours, so the rebalancer must touch very few tensors per interval, or use the tensor-selection path (see the measure/optimize/compile finding) instead of re-encoding.

findings.title: EXL3 requires a Hessian per linear (LDLQ, GPTQ-family) — and it is NEVER persisted to disk
findings.detail: `Linear.capture_H` accumulates `H.addmm_(x.T, x)` into a `(in_features, in_features)` fp32 matrix (linear.py:521,551). `finalize_capture_H` divides by count, damps the diagonal by `sigma_reg` (default 0.025) x mean, applies the su sign flips and the 128-point Hadamard to H, then takes a block-LDL/Cholesky decomposition with 10 damping retries (quantize.py:832-924, 411-485). `ldlq()` then sweeps k bottom-to-top in 16-row bands, feeding quantization error forward through `compensation_term.addmm_(bb_L.T, bb_err)` (quantize.py:544-599). Without a usable H the code falls back to `fallback_quant()` — plain per-tile trellis with no error feedback (quantize.py:607-722). Calibration defaults: 250 rows x 2048 columns = 512k tokens, from a fixed bundled mix (wiki 50, c4 20, code 20, random tokens 20, multilingual 10, technical 10, tiny 5) — `calibration_data.py:73-81`, `convert_model.py:179-180`. In `convert_model.py` the captured H is swapped to CPU (`v["H"] = v["H"].cpu()`, L1107-1109) and then dropped with `capture_H = None` (L1143). Nothing writes H to disk.
findings.relevance: This is the concrete blocker for online re-encoding: you cannot re-encode a single expert at a new K without its Hessian, and today the Hessian is computed during a strictly sequential layer-by-layer pass and thrown away. A fungible-quant implementation must either (a) persist Hessians as part of the cached quant state, or (b) recapture them live — which is exactly what the user's glm52-mtp78-collector plugin already demonstrates is feasible during serving.

findings.title: Hessian sizes and sharing for a GLM MoE layer are surprisingly tractable — and reveal EXL3 ignores routing entirely
findings.detail: In `BlockSparseMLP`, gate and up projections of ALL experts share one qmap `"{qmap}.input"` (block_sparse_mlp.py:477,495) — one Hessian of shape (hidden, hidden) for the whole expert bank. Down projections get a per-expert qmap `"{qmap}.{idx}.down"` (L512) — one (intermediate, intermediate) Hessian each. For GLM-class dims (hidden 5120, moe_intermediate 1536, 256 experts): shared gate/up H = 100 MiB; per-expert down H = 9.0 MiB x 256 = 2.25 GiB; ~2.35 GiB per MoE layer. Critically, capture runs with `"activate_all_experts": model.calibration_all_experts` (convert_model.py:1059, and `activate_all_experts: True` throughout measure_model.py) — so every expert sees the SAME token distribution and EXL3 deliberately does not weight experts by how often the router actually picks them.
findings.relevance: Two things fall out. (1) The Hessian state you would need to cache to make online re-encode possible is ~2.35 GiB/layer, ~210 GiB for a 90-layer GLM — large but disk-cacheable, and the shared gate/up H means 2/3 of the tensors need only ONE matrix per layer. (2) EXL3's own bit-allocation signal is routing-blind by construction. The user's live routed-expert statistics are precisely the information upstream throws away, which is the strongest argument that the fungible-quant idea adds real value rather than duplicating existing allocation.

findings.title: Bit allocation IS per-tensor, integer-only (K in 1..8), and mixed-K checkpoints are natively supported
findings.detail: `create_q_strategy()` returns `{module.key: target_bpw}` — one integer K per Linear module. `base_bpw = int(math.floor(bpw))`; the remaining budget is spent one whole bit at a time via `increase_1()` clamped to 8. A fractional model bpw (e.g. 3.42) is achieved purely by MIXING integer-K tensors, never by fractional coding. The checkpoint records it per module: `create_quantization_config_json` writes `module_dict["bits_per_weight"] = shape[-1] // 16` into `quantization_config.json` -> `tensor_storage`. At load, `LinearEXL3.__init__` does `self.K = trellis.shape[-1] // 16` (exl3.py:66) — K is inferred from the tensor's own shape, per tensor. Kernel dispatch validates `K >= 1 && K <= 8` (reconstruct.cu:162 etc.).
findings.relevance: Direct answer to 'is bit allocation per tensor': yes, and the format already carries per-tensor K with no extra machinery. A rebalancer only ever chooses integers from {2,3,4,5,6,...,8} per tensor — the search space is small and discrete, which makes a knapsack/greedy allocator natural.

findings.title: Exact K3 vs K4 shape/layout delta: pure K bits/weight, zero K-dependent metadata, dense packing mandatory
findings.detail: `pack_trellis` produces `packed_shape = (tiles_k, tiles_n, 256 * K // 16)` int16 = `(k/16, n/16, 16*K)`. Bytes = k*n*K/8 EXACTLY — no scale/zero-point overhead scaling with K. Per 16x16 tile: K2=64 B, K3=96 B, K4=128 B, K5=160 B, K6=192 B, K8=256 B. The pack kernel uses "16 spans of 16 weights to guarantee alignment for any K" (pack.cu:28-29), so every span of 16 weights is exactly K int16 words and the layout is 16-bit-word aligned for all K. The K-INVARIANT companion tensors are `suh` (in_features, fp16) and `svh` (out_features, fp16) — same SHAPE for any K, but their VALUES change on re-encode because `su /= g_scale` and g_scale is K-dependent. Plus optional scalar int32 `mcg`/`mul1` codebook markers. For a 5120x1536 GLM expert tensor: K3 = 2.812 MiB, K4 = 3.750 MiB (delta 0.938 MiB), suh 10 KiB, svh 3 KiB.
findings.relevance: The atomic swap unit is one contiguous trellis tensor plus two tiny fp16 vectors. The K3->K4 delta for one GLM expert tensor is under 1 MiB, so an arena can be sized in small increments. But note suh/svh must be swapped atomically WITH the trellis — a torn update between them silently corrupts the layer with no error.

findings.title: A K_max arena cannot be a padded tensor — kernel strides are compile-time-derived from K
findings.detail: In `exl3_gemm_inner.cuh` the trellis strides are computed from the template parameter `bits` with no runtime stride argument: `int gl_b_stride_k = blocks_n * TILEBLOCKS_K * 256 / 16 * bits;` (L127), `const int gl_b_stride_n = TILEBLOCKS_N * 256 / 16 * bits;` (L128), `sh_b_stage_size = TILEBLOCKS_K * TILEBLOCKS_N * 256 / 16 * bits` (L43), and the shared-memory dq offset `(sub_k * TILEBLOCKS_N + sub_n2) * 256 / 16 * bits` (L292). The host side derives K from the tensor itself: `int K = B.size(2) / 16;` (exl3_gemm.cu:161). So the kernel assumes a DENSELY packed tensor whose last dim is exactly 16*K. A tensor allocated at 16*K_max and used as a K3 tensor would be misread as garbage.
findings.relevance: Answers the arena question concretely. A fixed-capacity arena must be a raw byte pool (e.g. one big `torch.empty(bytes, dtype=uint8)` per layer) from which you carve DENSE views of shape (k/16, n/16, 16*K) via `.view(torch.int16).view(shape)` at the right offset. Sizing for K_max=4 across 256 experts x 3 tensors x 3.75 MiB = 2.81 GiB per MoE layer, with K3 occupancy leaving 25% of each slot idle — that idle 25% IS the memory cost of fungibility unless you compact, and compaction reintroduces fragmentation. Also: the pointer tables (`MultiLinear.ptrs_trellis`, multilinear.py:32) are baked `data_ptr()` values, so writing in place at a stable arena address is strongly preferable to reallocating.

findings.title: HARD BLOCKER upstream: an MoE expert bank must have uniform K (assert, not fallback)
findings.detail: `MultiLinear.__init__` asserts `self.K = linears[0].inner.K; assert all(l.inner.K == self.K for l in linears)` (multilinear.py:25-26). `BlockSparseMLP` builds `multi_gate`/`multi_up`/`multi_down` unconditionally whenever `support_quant_paths or support_bc_bsz1` (block_sparse_mlp.py:782-785), and `support_quant_paths` is true for any quantized silu/gelu gated MoE with no biases (L758-763) — i.e. always true for GLM. So upstream exllamav3 will hard-assert on a mixed-per-expert-K checkpoint; there is no soft fallback. The CUDA side agrees: `exl3_moe.cu` takes scalar `K_gate, K_up, K_down` and picks `exl3_moe_kernel_instances[4 * K + 2 * cb_idx + N_off]`, with `int K = 0; if (K_gate == K_up && K_up == K_down) K = K_gate;` — the K=0 variant switches K at runtime only BETWEEN the three projections, never between experts.
findings.relevance: This is the single largest engineering obstacle to per-expert fungible quantization, and it is a kernel-architecture constraint rather than a format constraint. The format happily stores per-expert K; the fused megakernel cannot consume it. Any design must either (a) drop to the per-expert non-fused path (large throughput loss), or (b) do what the GG fork already did — partition experts into K-tiers and run one megakernel per tier.

findings.title: The GG fork already implements two-tier mixed-K MoE — and it bakes the tier partition into contiguous slabs
findings.detail: `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/exl3.py` on `gg/dev/gilded-gnosis` (commit e2666d9a) carries a `_prepare_mixed_rank_sliced_weights()` path that: reads a per-expert bitrate vector from a `bits_per_expert` JSON reference (`file.json:field`, one entry per expert per layer, K in {3,4,5,6}); partitions experts into tiers with `if len(tiers) != 2: raise ValueError("the one-grid mixed Trellis path currently requires exactly two bitrates")`; for each tier `torch.stack`s all that tier's expert trellis tensors into ONE contiguous slab of shape `(2, n_tier, hidden/16, interm/16, 16*bits)` for w13 and `(n_tier, interm/16, hidden/16, 16*bits)` for w2; calls `b12x...mixed_trellis.prepare_weights(...)` per tier; then builds `global_to_combined` and `descriptor_map` remaps via `api.build_tiered_maps(tier_ids[0], tier_ids[1])`; and finally CLEARS the per-expert source tensors (`param.exl3_tensors.clear(); param.exl3_backing = None`). Tensor schema is `model.layers.{L}.mlp.experts.{E}.{proj}.rank{r}.{trellis|suh|svh|mcg}` — sharded per TP RANK in the checkpoint, requiring `codebook == "mcg"`.
findings.relevance: Three consequences for the fungible-quant design. (1) The seam already exists: the bits_per_expert JSON is exactly the artifact a rebalancer would rewrite. (2) But changing ONE expert's K today means rebuilding BOTH tier slabs (an expert must physically move between contiguous slabs) plus the global_to_combined/descriptor maps — this is the real 'atomic swap memory' cost, far larger than the ~1 MiB per-tensor delta. (3) `rank{r}` in the schema means the current quant is baked to the TP topology, directly contradicting the stated 'topology neutral' goal; the underlying EXL3 format is topology-neutral (trellis slices at 16-column granularity, exl3.py:303) but the GG storage layout is not.

findings.title: exllamav3 ALREADY ships an error-based automatic allocator — measure.py / optimize.py / compile.py
findings.detail: Three-stage pipeline that upstream does not advertise in the README. (1) `measure_model.py`: takes a BF16 reference dir plus >=2 already-quantized dirs at different bitrates, streams calibration state through all of them in lockstep, and for each module group measures the end-of-model KL-divergence delta from swapping that group up to a higher-bitrate variant. Granularity is set by `-l/--level` 0-3 via `optimizer_targets()` flattening — level 2 = per layer, level 3 = per tensor. (2) `optimize_model.py:optimize()` is a greedy knapsack maximizing `1e10 * dkld / (dbits + 1)`, with a concavity correction `adjust(dkld) = -((-dkld) ** 0.69)`. (3) `compile.py` builds the mixed checkpoint via `VariantSafetensorsCollection`: `vstc.add_stc([k + ".*" for k in keys], config.stc)` — it SELECTS tensors from the pre-quantized input directories and writes them out. NO RE-ENCODING HAPPENS. Community-reported measurement cost (mratsim, GLM-4.7-EXL3): "2 hours to 5 hours if comparing 2 quants -- to 12 hours if comparing 3 quants -- to 24h of compute if comparing all quants", with the caveat that "manual tuning using the heuristics below can achieve better KL-divergence than optimizing by only mixing 3 quants".
findings.relevance: This is the most important strategic finding. It shows the CHEAP implementation of fungible quant: do not re-encode at runtime at all. Keep a K3 checkpoint and a K4 checkpoint on disk (or stream the needed variant from HF, exactly as the user proposed), and make the periodic rebalance a pure TENSOR SUBSTITUTION — memcpy a 3.75 MiB K4 tensor over a 2.81 MiB K3 slot in the arena. That sidesteps the Hessian-persistence problem, the Viterbi cost, and the whole 'quantize online' machinery. The bit-allocation DECISION (the part the user calls unsolved) is what measure.py addresses offline; live routing statistics would replace the 2-24h offline KL sweep.

findings.title: Upstream's automatic allocator does NOT go per-expert — it groups the whole expert bank
findings.detail: `BlockSparseMLP.optimizer_targets()` returns `[s, [g + u, d]]` where g, u, d are the concatenated target lists of ALL experts' gates, ups and downs (block_sparse_mlp.py:617-626). So even at `-l3` the finest MoE granularity is 'layer L, all experts, gate+up' and 'layer L, all experts, down' — never 'layer L, expert 47'. The only per-tensor knobs upstream offers are the CLI flags `-b/--bits` (float target avg), `-hb/--head_bits` (int, default 6, lm_head), `-mb/--mtp_bits` (int, default 4, MTP layers), and `-hq/--hq` which applies a hardcoded per-module-class bump via `select_hq_bits`: attention +2, shared experts +2, dense MLP +1, routed experts +0 (glm4_moe.py:118,137,170; mlp.py:46; allocation.py:72,144-147). Promotion order is `(-priority, distance to nearer end of the forward pass, layer, idx)` — end layers get bits first (allocation.py:112-128).
findings.relevance: Confirms the user's premise that per-expert bit allocation is genuinely unsolved territory, not something already handled. Upstream has no per-expert allocator, no per-expert error measurement, and its calibration deliberately activates all experts uniformly. Note `-mb/--mtp_bits` defaults to 4 and is a first-class allocation category — directly relevant to the user's MTP layer 78 work, which used K3.

findings.title: There IS a single-module re-quantize API, but no CLI and no isolated whole-pipeline path
findings.detail: `Linear.convert_exl3(H_data, quant_args, ...)` (linear.py:463-516) is a genuine per-module entry point: it takes the module's own FP16 inner weight (`self.inner.get_weight_tensor().float()`), an H_data dict, and a quant_args dict containing K/seed/sigma_reg/devices; it calls `quantize_exl3()` and replaces `self.inner` with a fresh `LinearEXL3`. `quantize_exl3()` itself (quantize.py:1234-1432) is fully self-contained. However there is no CLI for it, and the conversion DRIVER is strictly sequential: layer N's calibration state comes from the already-quantized layers 0..N-1 (`advance_state_parallel`, convert_model.py:732+), Hessians are captured per layer and freed (L1143), and `convert_exl3` asserts `isinstance(self.inner, LinearFP16)` — you must reload the original BF16 weight, you cannot re-encode from an existing EXL3 tensor. `H_data` may also carry a `is_meta` H, which routes to the uncalibrated `fallback_quant` path (quantize.py:835-846, 607-722).
findings.relevance: Good news for the mechanics: a background thread can call quantize_exl3() on one tensor with a cached H and a streamed BF16 weight, producing exactly the tensors a hot swap needs. Bad news: the quality guarantee of the sequential pass is lost. LDLQ error feedback is intra-tensor (along k) only — `quantize_exl3_batch` states 'LDLQ treats columns independently given L' — but the layer-by-layer state advance means downstream layers were calibrated against the OLD upstream error, so changing an upstream expert's K makes downstream Hessians subtly stale.

findings.title: Multi-GPU encode is already built in and would map onto the user's 4x Blackwell box
findings.detail: `quantize_tiles_multigpu()` fans tiles out through PINNED host memory to N GPUs on per-device streams and gathers results back (quantize.py:170-302). The doc notes this "does not affect memory usage on the first GPU, and very little memory is used on the others, since only the most compute intensive operation (trellis encoding) is distributed". Device split ratios are autotuned by an EMA-damped `AutoSplit` class with per-architecture priors (`arch_prior_speed`: Hopper/Blackwell 5.0, Ada 4.0, Ampere 2.0). Parallel mode is now the default: one linear per device when a layer has >= n_devices tensors, else tile-splitting with small tensors capped at ~1M weights per device.
findings.relevance: An online re-encoder on the GG box could push trellis encoding to whichever GPUs are least loaded, using pinned host staging that never touches the serving GPUs' allocator. The ~1M-weights-per-device feed cap matters: a single 7.86M-weight expert tensor can usefully occupy at most ~8 devices, so 4 GPUs is a good match and would cut the ~1.5 s per-tensor encode toward ~0.4 s.

findings.title: Runtime already tolerates per-tensor K for non-MoE linears, including under tensor parallelism
findings.detail: `LinearEXL3` reads K from its own trellis (`self.K = trellis.shape[-1] // 16`) and passes it as a runtime int to `ext.BC_LinearEXL3(...)` and to `ext.reconstruct(w, self.trellis, self.K, self.mcg, self.mul1)` (exl3.py:66,81-90,195-210). TP import slices the trellis along dim 0 or dim 1 in units of 16 (`slice_dim = 1, first = first // 16, last = last // 16`, exl3.py:303,310,362) — proof that a trellis tensor can be cut at 16-column boundaries and remain valid, because each 16x16 tile is a self-contained tail-biting codeword. `suh`/`svh` slice correspondingly. Kernel dispatch accepts K in 1..8 for all paths.
findings.relevance: Confirms 'topology neutral' is achievable at the FORMAT level: a per-tensor-K EXL3 checkpoint stored unsharded can be sliced to any TP degree at load time at 16-column granularity, with no re-encode. The GG fork's `rank{r}` pre-sharding is a storage/loading choice, not a format limitation — worth flagging as the concrete thing to change if topology neutrality is a requirement.

findings.title: Bounding the memory cost of a K_max arena for the user's actual model
findings.detail: Using GLM-class dims (hidden 5120, moe_intermediate 1536, 256 routed experts, top-8): per-expert trellis at K3 = 3 x 2.812 MiB = 8.44 MiB; at K4 = 3 x 3.750 MiB = 11.25 MiB. Per MoE layer: K3 bank = 2.11 GiB, K4 bank = 2.81 GiB, so an arena sized for K_max=4 costs +0.70 GiB per layer over an all-K3 bank (+33%). Across TP4 that is per-rank /4. If the current mix is, say, 25% K4 / 75% K3, the incremental headroom to make ALL experts upgradable is +0.53 GiB/layer. Metadata is negligible: suh+svh = 13 KiB per tensor, ~10 MiB per 256-expert layer.
findings.relevance: Quantifies the user's stated concern about 'memory reserved for atomic swap'. Two viable postures: (a) size every slot at K_max and eat a flat ~33% overhead on the MoE bank, which makes swaps address-stable (critical because MultiLinear caches raw data_ptr()s) and eliminates fragmentation entirely; or (b) keep slots tight and pay a per-swap staging buffer of one tensor (3.75 MiB) plus a slab rebuild if the GG two-tier layout is retained. Option (a) is far simpler and its cost is bounded and predictable — but note it directly consumes the headroom that made 3.0-3.42 bpw attractive in the first place, so the honest framing is 'K_max arena at 33% overhead vs just quantizing more experts at K4 outright'.
findings.citation: Derived from exllamav3/modules/quant/exl3_lib/quantize.py:932 (packed_shape = (k/16, n/16, 256*K/16) int16) and exllamav3/modules/multilinear.py:32; dims per GLM-4.x config conventions

gaps: No published wall-clock benchmark isolates encode time for a SINGLE tensor at K3 vs K4 on the same hardware. My ~5M weights/s figure is derived from issue #112 conversion logs at 5.76 bpw (mostly K5/K6) on an UNSTATED GPU; the K-independence of Viterbi compute is proven from the kernel source, but the +17% K>=4 occupancy bump on Blackwell and the small-tensor underfill effect (k_proj ran at only 3.1M w/s) mean real K3-vs-K4 timings could differ by tens of percent. Recommend measuring directly with quantize_exl3() on one 5120x1536 tensor.

There is no formal specification of the EXL3 format. doc/exl3.md says only 'A full description of the format is coming' and refers the reader to the source. Everything about the bitstream in this report is read out of the CUDA/Python source at commit 4f8ad012, not from a spec, so it is subject to change without a compatibility guarantee.

The b12x / SparkInfer mixed_trellis kernel source is NOT reachable from this session (only malaiwah/vllm-voipmonitor and malaiwah/glm52-mtp78-collector are authorized). I read only the vLLM-side caller in the GG fork. I could not determine: whether run_mixed_trellis supports more than 2 tiers, whether prepare_weights copies or aliases the stacked slab (which decides whether an in-place hot swap into the arena is even visible to the kernel), whether tier membership can change without recompiling the launch, or what the throughput penalty of the two-tier path is versus uniform K.

I did not find any published measurement of the QUALITY delta between K3 and K4 for an individual routed expert, nor any evidence about how much per-expert (as opposed to per-layer) bit allocation actually buys. Upstream's own allocator never goes below per-layer-per-projection granularity, so there is no upstream data point on whether the fungible-quant idea's core premise pays off.

I could not determine how much a re-encoded expert's quality degrades when using a STALE Hessian, or one captured at a different point in the sequential conversion. LDLQ error feedback is intra-tensor, but the layer-by-layer state advance means downstream layers were calibrated against the pre-change upstream error. Whether this matters at the scale of one expert out of 256 is unmeasured and would need an experiment.

No exllamav3 mechanism exists for per-tile or per-column-block K within one tensor, and I found no evidence anyone has tried it. The encoder works tile-by-tile so it is structurally possible, but the runtime kernels derive all strides from a single compile-time `bits`, so it would require new kernels.

Hessian persistence: I confirmed nothing writes H to disk in the conversion path, but I did not audit the checkpoint/resume format (save_dict/load_tensor in convert_model.py) closely enough to rule out that H is incidentally serialized into work-dir checkpoints. Worth a direct check if Hessian caching becomes the chosen design.

I did not verify whether the GG fork's `bits_per_expert` JSON map is regenerable by any tool the user controls, or how the existing K3/K4 assignment for GLM-5.2 was originally decided — the mratsim GLM-4.7 model card references a 'qwen3.5-override-13.yaml' mixing recipe that suggests hand-tuned per-module overrides outside the upstream toolchain, but I could not retrieve that file.
